parsed.overview: JPMorgan Chase reported strong second-quarter 2026 financial results driven by robust performance across markets, investment banking, asset management, and deposit balances.
keyTakeaways: The firm delivered net income of $16.9 billion, EPS of $6.14, and an ROTCE of 23% for the second quarter of 2026.
Management noted that consumers and small businesses continue to show resilience, with strong spend growth supported by a solid labor market and higher tax refunds.
The board intends to increase the quarterly dividend to $1.65 per share effective in the third quarter.
Management announced leadership updates, including the elevation of Doug and Troy to co-presidents.
Active client engagement and favorable dynamic market conditions drove exceptionally strong performance in equities and fixed income within the CIB.
financialHighlights: Excluding significant items, revenue rose 15% year-on-year, driven by markets revenue, higher asset management fees, higher investment banking revenue, and higher deposit and loan balances.
Expenses were $27.3 billion, up 15% year-on-year, driven by volume and revenue-related expenses, front office hiring, and labor inflation.
Credit costs were $2.5 billion, consisting of net charge-offs of $2.4 billion and a net reserve build of $149 million.
The standardized CET1 ratio ended the quarter at 14.1%, down 20 basis points versus the prior quarter.

CIB reported net income of $9.7 billion on revenue of $24.9 billion, which was up 27% year-on-year.
AWM reported net income of $2 billion on revenue of $6.9 billion, with long-term net inflows of $50 billion and AUM reaching $5.1 trillion.
guidance: Management expects full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets to be about $96.5 billion.
Total NII for full-year 2026 is projected at approximately $105.5 billion, with markets NII increasing to about $9 billion.
The full-year 2026 adjusted expense outlook is revised to about $107.5 billion.
Management expects the full-year card net charge-off rate to be approximately 3.2%.
analystFocus: Analysts questioned the sustainability of elevated capital markets and investment banking activity levels.
Inquiries were made regarding deposit growth, retail market share aspirations, and deposit beta behavior in a higher-for-longer rate environment.
Discussions focused on CEO succession timing, leadership changes, and desirable characteristics for future leadership.
Analysts asked about expense growth, operating leverage, and the potential long-term efficiencies driven by AI and technology investments.
Questions were raised regarding regulatory proposals, capital deployment, and potential M&A or buyback strategies.
risksMentioned: Management highlighted potential yield-seeking deposit flows and deposit pricing convexity as ongoing risks.
Uncertainties surrounding macroeconomic fragility, inflation, and labor market resilience were discussed as factors that could impact consumer credit performance.
Management noted risks related to regulatory changes, capital requirements, and short-term wholesale funding rules.

parsed.overview: Apple reported fiscal Q3 2026 revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% year-over-year, driven by record iPhone, Mac, and Services revenue despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds.
keyTakeaways: CEO Tim Cook announced that fiscal Q3 2026 was his final earnings call, with incoming CEO John Ternus leading future calls.
Apple announced a multi-year agreement with Broadcom expected to exceed $30 billion to design and produce custom silicon and wireless connectivity technologies in the U.S.
Apple launched Apple Upgrade in the U.S. in partnership with Klarna, offering customers a hardware leasing program.
Apple announced plans to reinvest its tariff refunds into the U.S. supply chain and advanced manufacturing facilities, including the Apple Advanced Manufacturing Center in Houston.

Diluted earnings per share reached $2.02, up 29% year-over-year, which included a $0.11 favorable impact from tariff refunds.
Gross margin was 50.1%, including a two percentage point benefit from tariff refunds.
guidance: Management expects total company revenue for the September quarter to grow between 9% and 11% year-over-year.

analystFocus: Analysts focused on the drivers and duration of supply constraints, which management attributed to unexpectedly high demand and limited supply chain flexibility for advanced silicon nodes.
Analysts questioned the impact of memory price inflation, which management highlighted as the primary factor driving sequential gross margin compression.
Analysts inquired about the rollout timeline and regulatory approval process for Siri AI in Europe and China Mainland.
Analysts sought details regarding the Apple Upgrade leasing program and its potential effect on product replacement cycles.
risksMentioned: Management highlighted severe supply constraints on advanced semiconductor nodes impacting iPhone, Mac, and iPad availability.
Management cited sequential foreign exchange headwinds affecting overall revenue and services growth rates.
Management warned that increasing memory market pricing could create continued cost pressures on product gross margins beyond the September quarter.

parsed.overview: Apple reported fiscal Q3 2026 (June quarter) revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% year-over-year, with management guiding September quarter revenue growth of 9%-11% year-over-year amid supply constraints and FX headwinds. Tim Cook said this would be his final earnings call, with John Ternus to lead future calls.
keyTakeaways: Total revenue of $109.4 billion was up 16% year-over-year and was a June quarter record.
iPhone revenue grew 22% year-over-year to $54.3 billion, with management citing the iPhone 17 family.
Mac revenue grew 29% year-over-year to $10.4 billion despite significant supply constraints.
Services revenue grew 12% year-over-year to $30.7 billion, a June quarter record.
Management said supply constraints on advanced SoC nodes are expected to increase significantly sequentially in the September quarter, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad.
Management said memory costs are expected to be higher in the September quarter, partly offset by carry-in inventory and lower non-memory component costs.
Management said it reluctantly raised prices on some products due to memory pricing increases.
Tim Cook said this is his final earnings call and John Ternus will lead future calls.
financialHighlights: Products revenue was $78.7 billion, up 18% year-over-year.
Company gross margin was 50.1%, up 80 basis points sequentially, including a benefit of about two percentage points from tariff refunds.
Products gross margin was 40.1%, up 140 basis points sequentially, including a tariff refund benefit of over two and a half percentage points.
Services gross margin was 75.6%, down 110 basis points sequentially due to mix.
Operating expenses were $19.1 billion, up 23% year-over-year, driven by R&D investments.
Net income was $29.8 billion and diluted EPS was $2.02, up 29% year-over-year, including $0.11 from tariff refunds.
Operating cash flow was $34.4 billion.
iPad revenue was $6.2 billion, down 6% year-over-year.
Wearables, home and accessories revenue was $7.9 billion, up 6% year-over-year.
Cash and marketable securities totaled $147 billion and total debt was $84 billion.
During the quarter Apple returned $33 billion to shareholders, including $4 billion in dividends and equivalents and $25.8 billion in share repurchases.
Installed base exceeded 2.5 billion active devices and paid subscriptions surpassed 1.5 billion.
guidance: Management expects September quarter total company revenue to grow 9%-11% year-over-year.
Management expects FX to be a sequential headwind of about 2.5 percentage points to year-over-year total company growth from the June to September quarter.
Management expects iPhone reported revenue growth in the September quarter to be mid-teens year-over-year.
Management expects services year-over-year reported growth in the September quarter to be largely similar to June after removing about a 2.5 point sequential FX headwind.

parsed.overview: Apple reported fiscal Q3 2026 (June quarter) revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% year over year and a June quarter record, despite supply constraints and sequential FX headwinds; this was Tim Cook's final earnings call, with John Ternus to lead future calls.
keyTakeaways: Management said revenue set June quarter records in every geographic segment, with double-digit growth in every segment.
iPhone revenue grew 22% and Mac grew 29%, while iPad declined 6% against a difficult prior-year launch compare.
Management said supply constraints, mainly advanced-node SoC availability, hit Mac most, and iPhone and iPad to a lesser extent, in the June quarter.
Management attributed the constraints to demand running above its forecasts for iPhone and Mac, with less flexibility in the supply chain than normal.
Management said memory costs rose significantly in the June quarter and expects higher memory costs in September, with market pricing continuing to increase beyond that.
Tim Cook described the memory price increases as a '100-year flood' and said Apple reluctantly raised prices.

Management said Siri AI beta feedback has been overwhelmingly positive; it may not launch in the EU on iPhone and iPad, though it is offered or will be offered on Mac there, and China needs more work.
Apple announced the Apple Upgrade leasing program with Klarna, available only in the U.S. and offered in Apple retail stores.
Apple announced a Broadcom agreement expected to exceed $30 billion, its largest American manufacturing program commitment.
financialHighlights: Revenue was $109.4 billion, up 16% year over year; Products revenue was $78.7 billion, up 18%.
iPhone revenue was $54.3 billion, up 22%; Mac was $10.4 billion, up 29%; iPad was $6.2 billion, down 6%; Wearables, Home and Accessories was $7.9 billion, up 6%.
Services revenue was $30.7 billion, up 12%, a June quarter record, with all-time records in cloud services and payment services.
Company gross margin was 50.1%, up 80 basis points sequentially, including a tariff refund benefit of approximately two percentage points.
Products gross margin was 40.1% (up 140 basis points sequentially, including over 2.5 points from tariff refunds); Services gross margin was 75.6% (down 110 basis points sequentially).
Operating expenses were $19.1 billion, up 23% year over year, driven by R&D investment.
Net income was $29.8 billion and diluted EPS was $2.02, up 29%, including $0.11 of favorable tariff refund impact.
Operating cash flow was $34.4 billion.
Installed base exceeded 2.5 billion active devices, and paid subscriptions surpassed 1.5 billion.

Apple ended the quarter with $147 billion in cash and marketable securities and $84 billion in total debt, and returned $33 billion to shareholders, including $4 billion in dividends and $25.8 billion in buybacks.
The board declared a dividend of $0.27 per share, payable August 13, 2026 to holders of record August 10, 2026.
guidance: Management expects September quarter total revenue to grow 9%-11% year over year, assuming current tariffs remain in effect and the macro outlook does not worsen.
Management expects FX to be a sequential headwind of about 2.5 percentage points to total company growth, and supply constraint impact to increase significantly, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad.
Management expects iPhone reported growth in the September quarter to be mid-teens year over year.
Management expects Services reported growth to be largely similar to the June quarter's after removing the roughly 2.5 point sequential FX headwind.
Management expects gross margin of 47%-48%, including about one percentage point of benefit from tariff refunds.
Management expects operating expenses of $19.1 billion-$19.4 billion, OIE of around $350 million excluding mark-to-market of minority investments, and a tax rate of around 16.5%.
Management said it is not providing guidance or color beyond the September quarter.
analystFocus: Analysts asked how much of the guided deceleration comes from supply constraints versus FX, and which constraints are broadening.
Analysts asked about memory cost inflation, sourcing flexibility and the rationale behind price increases.
Analysts asked about Apple Upgrade adoption and whether Siri AI will drive iPhone demand and compute cost recovery via iCloud+.
Analysts asked about December quarter impact from supply constraints and whether silicon suppliers could be broadened.
Analysts asked about the Services deceleration, including App Store and mobile gaming trends.
Analysts asked about possible demand pull-forward, AI capital intensity, competitive landscape, Siri AI rollout in the EU and China, and the gross margin walk.
risksMentioned: Supply constraints from limited advanced-node SoC availability and a less flexible supply chain.
Rising memory costs, with only three DRAM suppliers and market pricing expected to keep increasing; management said carry-in inventory benefits should decrease beyond September.
Tariffs and other trade measures, and macroeconomic conditions.
Foreign exchange headwinds, particularly for Services.
Services headwinds including softer mobile gaming, App Store business model changes, and a U.S. court ruling on link-out transactions, with a Supreme Court appeal to be heard.
Uncertain price elasticity from price increases on Mac and iPad.
Regulatory constraints on Siri AI in the EU and further required work in China.
Uncertain compute costs of Siri AI and the extent to which iCloud+ upgrades offset them.

parsed.overview: JPMorgan Chase's second quarter 2026 earnings call covered record-level markets and investment banking results, a raised full-year 2026 NII and expense outlook, management succession commentary, deposit and rate sensitivity, regulatory views, and AI-related efficiency themes.
keyTakeaways: Management reported net income of $16.9 billion, EPS of $6.14 and ROTCE of 23% for the quarter.
Excluding significant items, revenue rose 15% year-on-year, predominantly driven by markets revenue.
The board intends to increase the quarterly dividend to $1.65 per share, effective in the third quarter.
Management now expects full-year 2026 adjusted expense of about $107.5 billion, up from prior guidance mainly due to volume and revenue-related expenses.
Management expects card net charge-off rate of approximately 3.2%, reflecting better-than-expected consumer credit performance.
Management said the equities business revenue was up 86% year-on-year, though it views the specific set of drivers this quarter as unlikely to repeat in the same combination.
Management stated that Troy and Doug were elevated to co-presidents and that Marianne's retirement was her own decision, with the succession timetable unchanged.
financialHighlights: Revenue of $20.3 billion in CCB, up 8% year-on-year, with net income of $5.3 billion.
CIB revenue of $24.9 billion, up 27% year-on-year, with net income of $9.7 billion and IB fees up 30% year-on-year.
IB fees grew double digits across all products, with particularly strong equity underwriting performance.
Fixed income revenue in markets was up 6% year-on-year.
AWM revenue of $6.9 billion, up 19% year-on-year, with pre-tax margin of 38% and long-term net inflows of $50 billion.
AUM of $5.1 trillion was up 18% year-on-year and client assets of $7.7 trillion were up 19% year-on-year.
Expenses of $27.3 billion were up 15% year-on-year, and credit costs were $2.5 billion with net charge-offs of $2.4 billion.
Standardized CET1 ratio was 14.1%, down 20 basis points quarter-on-quarter, with standardized RWA rising about $103 billion.
Full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets is now expected at about $96.5 billion, up from $95 billion, and total NII at about $105.5 billion with markets NII of about $9 billion.
Management said first-half capital markets revenue outperformed expectations by $6.5 billion and $1.5 billion of associated expenses were booked, with $1 billion implicitly added for the second half.
Consumer deposits grew 3% year-on-year on average, and over 500,000 net new checking accounts were added this quarter.
guidance: Management expects NII ex-Markets of about $96.5 billion for full-year 2026, assuming forward yield curve and current deposit expectations.
Management expects total NII of approximately $105.5 billion for full-year 2026.
Management expects adjusted expense of about $107.5 billion for full-year 2026.
Management expects card net charge-off rate of approximately 3.2% for 2026.
Management expects consumer deposit growth to remain low single-digit this year.
Management expects investment banking activity levels to remain healthy, while noting conversion depends on market conditions.
Management expects token expense to accelerate meaningfully in the second half of 2026 but remain trivial for the full year.
Management expects a new consumer smart cash tool to be seen this year.
Management expects the 15% retail deposit market share to be a natural outcome of strategy, with no change to that aspiration.
analystFocus: Sustainability of investment banking and markets strength, and how much pull forward occurred this quarter.
Retail deposit market share progression and the effect of higher-for-longer rates on deposit pace.
Operating leverage outlook, expense investment cycle and the role of AI in future expense growth.
Drivers of the NII ex-Markets upward revision and exit run rate into next year.
Deposit betas and the potential for negative convexity in consumer deposits at higher rate levels.
Management succession, qualities sought in a future CEO, and Troy's suitability for the consumer bank role.
Regulatory proposals including G-SIB surcharge, market risk capital, operational risk capital and short-term wholesale funding.
Share buyback approach at current valuation levels and potential inorganic deployment.
Credit underwriting standards in competitive lending markets, notably data center financing.
Consumer health, including labor market dependence and any K-shape or real wage concerns.
CIB capital allocation and whether allocation is at peak.
risksMentioned: Management noted some pull forward of investment banking activity and that this quarter's equity results included exceptional events unlikely to repeat.
Management stated that the market environment is highly dynamic and that durability of current activity levels is not known.
Management flagged that consumer yield-seeking deposit flows are a risk and that deposit convexity could emerge in a higher-rate stress scenario.
Management highlighted that some lenders are showing mild underwriting weakness, including more PIK, weaker covenants and rollover risk.
Management noted a cohort of consumers may face negative real wage growth, which is a watch area.
Management noted that inflation is slightly above normal and that elevated gas prices are present.
Management flagged that liquidity in the banking system is at the margin less abundant, and that regulatory changes to short-term wholesale funding disproportionately affect universal banks.
Management noted that consumer credit performance depends heavily on the labor market.

parsed.overview: Apple reported fiscal Q3 2026 (June quarter) revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% year-over-year and a June quarter record, driven by iPhone (+22%) and Mac (+29%), with Services at a record $30.7 billion (+12%); management guided September quarter revenue growth of 9%-11%, citing significantly increasing supply constraints and FX headwinds, while memory cost inflation weighs on gross margin. This was Tim Cook's final earnings call, with incoming CEO John Ternus to lead future calls.
keyTakeaways: Revenue of $109.4 billion grew 16% year-over-year, with June quarter records in every geographic segment and double-digit growth in every segment despite supply constraints.
iPhone revenue reached $54.3 billion (+22%) and Mac $10.4 billion (+29%), both June quarter records, with IDC-reported global share gains in each.
Management said supply constraints stem from limited availability of advanced nodes for Apple's SoCs, which Tim Cook characterised as a demand-forecast issue rather than a supplier issue.

Management expects memory costs to rise further in the September quarter and said market memory pricing beyond September continues to increase, describing it as a '100-year flood' that led Apple to reluctantly raise prices, including on Mac and iPad.
Siri AI was unveiled at WWDC and is in developer and public beta, with management citing overwhelmingly positive feedback and planning iCloud+ upgrade options for heavy users.
Apple announced a multi-year Broadcom agreement expected to exceed $30 billion, its largest-ever American Manufacturing Program commitment, and plans to reinvest tariff refunds into the U.S.
Apple launched Apple Upgrade, a U.S.-only hardware leasing program with Klarna offered in retail stores.
Tim Cook confirmed this was his final earnings call, with John Ternus to lead future calls.
financialHighlights: Total revenue was $109.4 billion, up 16% year-over-year.
Products revenue was $78.7 billion, up 18%; Services revenue was $30.7 billion, up 12%.
iPhone revenue was $54.3 billion (+22%), Mac $10.4 billion (+29%), iPad $6.2 billion (-6%), and Wearables, Home and Accessories $7.9 billion (+6%).
Company gross margin was 50.1%, up 80 basis points sequentially, including an approximately 2 percentage point benefit from tariff refunds (about 48.1% excluding it).
Products gross margin was 40.1% (including over 2.5 points of tariff refund benefit) and Services gross margin was 75.6%, down 110 basis points sequentially on mix.
Operating expenses were $19.1 billion, up 23% year-over-year, driven by R&D investment.
Net income was $29.8 billion and diluted EPS was $2.02, up 29%, including $0.11 of tariff refund benefit.
Operating cash flow was $34.4 billion; net income, EPS and operating cash flow set June quarter records even excluding tariff refunds.
Cash and marketable securities were $147 billion against $84 billion total debt, and Apple returned $33 billion to shareholders including $4 billion in dividends and $25.8 billion in buybacks.
Installed base exceeds 2.5 billion active devices and paid subscriptions surpassed 1.5 billion.
Board declared a $0.27 per share dividend payable August 13, 2026 to holders of record August 10, 2026.
guidance: Management expects September quarter total revenue to grow 9%-11% year-over-year, assuming current tariff policies and no worsening macro outlook.

Management expects FX to be a sequential headwind of about 2.5 percentage points to the year-over-year total company growth rate, and supply constraint impact to increase significantly, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad.
Management expects iPhone reported growth of mid-teens year-over-year in the September quarter.

Management expects Services growth largely similar to the June quarter after removing a roughly 2.5 point sequential FX headwind, with FX a roughly 5 point headwind from the March to September quarter.
Management expects gross margin of 47%-48%, including approximately 1 percentage point of tariff refund benefit, with the sequential decline attributed mainly to memory costs.
Management expects operating expenses of $19.1 billion-$19.4 billion, OIE of around $350 million, and a tax rate of around 16.5%.
Management declined to provide any guidance beyond the September quarter.
analystFocus: Amit Daryanani (Evercore) asked how much of the September deceleration stems from supply versus FX and about memory sourcing; management attributed it to FX and advanced-node constraints and said it is evaluating all options given three main DRAM suppliers.

Michael Ng (Goldman Sachs) asked about Apple Upgrade adoption and Siri AI demand and compute costs; Cook said early feedback is positive and iCloud+ upgrade options are planned, but there is not yet a complete compute cost plan.

Ben Reitzes (Melius) asked about supply impact on December and broadening silicon suppliers; management gave no post-September guidance and stressed it is not a supplier issue, noting over 100 million components sourced from Arizona this year.

Erik Woodring (Morgan Stanley) asked about pricing philosophy and services deceleration; Cook said pricing weighs units, revenue and margin long-term, and Parekh cited FX, a prior-year F1 theatrical release, mobile gaming softness and App Store business model changes.
Aaron Rakers (Wells Fargo) asked about demand pull-forward; Cook said it is not obvious in the data and it is too early to judge price elasticity on Mac and iPad.
Wamsi Mohan (Bank of America) asked about Siri AI capital intensity and competition; Cook said the cost balance is uncertain under a hybrid model, and John Ternus said Apple is focused on its plans.

Samik Chatterjee (JPMorgan) asked about Siri AI in China and the EU and gross margin drivers; Cook cited ongoing work with the EU Commission and recent China approval for original Apple Intelligence features, and Parekh attributed over 100% of sequential margin declines to memory costs.
risksMentioned: Supply constraints on advanced nodes for SoCs, expected to increase significantly in the September quarter across iPhone, Mac and iPad.
Rising memory costs, with diminishing carry-in inventory benefit beyond the September quarter and market pricing continuing to increase.
Foreign exchange headwinds, particularly affecting Services.
Price elasticity uncertainty following price increases on Mac and iPad.
Mobile gaming softness and App Store business model changes, plus the U.S. court ruling on link-out transactions under appeal to the Supreme Court.
Regulatory hurdles delaying Siri AI on iPhone and iPad in the EU and requiring further work for Siri AI in China.
Uncertain AI compute costs and capital intensity from Siri AI.
Macroeconomic conditions, tariffs, and legal and regulatory proceedings cited in forward-looking statement disclaimers.

parsed.overview: JPMorgan Chase reported Q2 2026 net income of $16.9 billion, EPS of $6.14 and ROTCE of 23%, with revenue up 15% year-on-year excluding significant items, driven mainly by markets and investment banking. Management raised full-year NII and expense guidance and lowered its card net charge-off rate outlook. The Q&A covered management succession, expense and operating leverage, AI, capital deployment, regulation and credit underwriting.
keyTakeaways: Management attributed the revenue strength mainly to markets, higher asset management fees, higher investment banking revenue and higher deposit and loan balances, partly offset by lower rates.
Jeremy Barnum said investment banking benefited from some pull-forward and large deals, but the pipeline remains robust and management expects activity levels to remain healthy.
Barnum said the equities quarter was exceptionally strong and it is statistically improbable that the same combination of effects would repeat.
Jamie Dimon said the environment is getting close to as good as it gets, but that management does not know how long it will last.
Dimon said the board named two co-presidents (Doug and Troy), that Marianne chose to retire, and that the CEO succession timetable is essentially unchanged and up to the board.
Management said the $2.5 billion expense guidance increase is mostly volume- and revenue-related, with $1.5 billion already booked in the first half.
Dimon said AI efficiencies are expected in parts of the company but that the benefit will ultimately accrue largely to customers rather than margins.
Management said excess capital is mainly intended for organic deployment, and that buybacks are an investment decision rather than a return of money to shareholders.
financialHighlights: Net income was $16.9 billion, EPS $6.14 and ROTCE 23%, including significant items.
Revenue excluding significant items was up 15% year-on-year; expenses were $27.3 billion, up 15%.
Credit costs were $2.5 billion, with net charge-offs of $2.4 billion and a net reserve build of $149 million.
Standardized CET1 ratio was 14.1%, down 20 basis points quarter-on-quarter, with standardized RWA up about $103 billion.
The board intends to raise the quarterly dividend to $1.65 per share, effective in the third quarter.
CCB net income was $5.3 billion on revenue of $20.3 billion, up 8%, with over 500,000 net new checking accounts and client investment assets up 21%.
CIB net income was $9.7 billion on revenue of $24.9 billion, up 27%; IB fees were up 30%, fixed income up 6% and equities up 86%.
AWM net income was $2 billion with a 38% pre-tax margin on revenue of $6.9 billion, up 19%; long-term net inflows were $50 billion, AUM $5.1 trillion and client assets $7.7 trillion.
Corporate reported net income of $4.2 billion on revenue of $6 billion.
guidance: Management now expects full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets of about $96.5 billion, up from $95 billion previously.
Management expects total NII of approximately $105.5 billion, with markets NII rising to about $9 billion.
Management's new adjusted expense outlook is about $107.5 billion, up $2.5 billion, mainly on volume and revenue-related expenses.
Management now expects the card net charge-off rate to be approximately 3.2%, reflecting better-than-expected consumer credit performance.
Management said its expectation of low single-digit consumer deposit growth this year is unchanged.

Drivers of the NII ex-Markets and markets NII guidance revisions.
Expense growth, operating leverage and the investment cycle, including the AI and token expense outlook.
Regulatory proposals, including G-SIB surcharge, Basel III and short-term wholesale funding, and regulatory stability.
Capital deployment, buybacks, M&A, the CIB capital allocation and European consumer banking ambitions.
Underwriting standards and the health of the consumer.
risksMentioned: Management said yield-seeking deposit flows remain a factor and probably a little bit of a risk in a more hawkish rate environment.
Barnum said deposit rates paid could accelerate at some point, so higher rates should not be viewed naively.
Dimon said there has been mild weakening in credit underwriting across the market, such as more PIK, weaker covenants and more rollover risk, and that a credit cycle will come.
Barnum flagged consumers with negative real wage growth as a watch area and said consumer credit depends on the labor market.
Dimon said elevated market prices and volumes may not last.
Management said proposed regulatory treatment of operating risk, market risk, G-SIB and short-term wholesale funding would burden banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America.
Barnum said the system is less flush with liquidity at the margin and that this may require adjustments to liquidity regulation.

parsed.overview: Lilly reported fiscal Q2 2026 results with revenue up 48% versus Q2 2025, raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance, and reviewed progress across Foundayo launches, retatrutide development, pipeline additions and business development.
keyTakeaways: Management said revenue grew 48% versus Q2 2025 and the company raised its full-year 2026 guidance.
Management expects full-year 2026 revenue of $85 billion to $87 billion.
Management said U.S. price declined 9% excluding rebate and discount estimate adjustments, which contributed to U.S. price being down 3% reported.
Management said the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program launched July 1 and expanded coverage for obesity medicines by 35% in the U.S.
Management plans to submit retatrutide in the U.S. in Q1 2027 under a BLA pathway, noting a mixed court decision and ongoing CMC work.
Management said retatrutide Phase III TRIUMPH data support global registrations in obesity, obstructive sleep apnea and knee osteoarthritis pain.
Management said Foundayo is under regulatory review in over 40 countries and expects a global rollout in all major markets in 2027.
Management said business development remains active, with recent acquisitions including AtaiBeckley, Centessa, Curevo, LimmaTech and The Vaccine Company.
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 48% versus Q2 2025, driven by ZEPBOUND and MOUNJARO.
Gross margin was 86.3% of revenue, up approximately 1.3 percentage points versus Q2 2025.
Non-GAAP performance margin was 54.8%, up nine percentage points from Q2 2025.
Non-GAAP EPS was $8.38 including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges, versus $6.31 in Q2 2025.
U.S. revenue increased 33%, primarily driven by volume growth.
Europe revenue grew 55% in constant currency, including a $250 million Jardiance milestone payment.
China revenue grew 93% in constant currency and Japan grew 30% in constant currency.
MOUNJARO and ZEPBOUND combined for $14.9 billion of Q2 revenue, contributing $6.3 billion of growth versus Q2 2025.
Marketing, selling and administrative expenses increased 25% and R&D expenses increased 14%.
Management raised the low end of revenue guidance by $3 billion and the high end by $2 billion.
Management now expects a non-GAAP performance margin of 49% to 50.5%.
Management now expects non-GAAP EPS of $35.50 to $36.50, before the $3.03 Q2 acquired IPR&D impact.
Lilly distributed $1.5 billion in dividends and executed $1.6 billion in share repurchases in Q2.
guidance: Management expects full-year 2026 revenue of $85 billion to $87 billion.
Management expects non-GAAP performance margin of 49% to 50.5% for 2026.
Management expects non-GAAP EPS of $35.50 to $36.50 for 2026, before updating for Q2 acquired IPR&D charges of $3.03.
Management expects a seasonal revenue decline in Europe in Q3 due to holidays, which is factored into guidance.
Management expects further Foundayo regulatory approvals in additional markets later this year.
Management expects a Foundayo obstructive sleep apnea readout later this year.
Management expects EU approval of insulin efsitora alfa in the coming months.
Management expects regulatory action on Foundayo for Type 2 diabetes in the U.S. later this year.
analystFocus: Analysts asked about the depth of the consumer and self-pay obesity market in the U.S. versus outside the U.S.
Analysts asked about the slower-than-expected Foundayo U.S. launch curve and competitive dynamics ex-U.S. versus Novo Nordisk's oral launches.
Analysts asked about the retatrutide BLA regulatory pathway and whether other incretins could follow it.
Analysts asked about Medicare GLP-1 Bridge rollout learnings and the oral versus injectable mix.
Analysts asked about the back-half guidance implying slower revenue growth.
Analysts asked about net pricing for obesity medicines and the role of medical exceptions.
Analysts asked about generic semaglutide impacts on MOUNJARO in India, Brazil and Canada.
Analysts asked about the breast cancer strategy after Verzenio, the M&A strategy in psychiatry and vaccines, and pipeline assets outside obesity.
risksMentioned: Management said retatrutide's BLA pathway is subject to active litigation with the FDA and a mixed first court decision, and additional CMC work is needed.
Management said medical exceptions and CVS formulary changes are putting downward pressure on ZEPBOUND price, which management expects to offset with volume.
Management noted that early Foundayo sales data can be affected by sell-in and inventory build, making it noisy.
Management acknowledged generic semaglutide launches in markets such as India and Brazil, though it said tirzepatide TRx continued to grow.
Management noted a U.S. Q2 price benefit from rebate estimate changes that management does not expect to recur.
Management said ex-U.S. reimbursement always takes time.

Rising memory costs were a central theme, with management describing a '100-year flood' in memory pricing that drove reluctant price increases. This was Tim Cook's final earnings call as CEO, with incoming CEO John Ternus joining the call.
keyTakeaways: Revenue of $109.4 billion grew 16% year-over-year with June quarter records in every geographic segment and double-digit growth in every segment.
iPhone revenue grew 22% to $54.3 billion, driven by the iPhone 17 family, with a June quarter record for upgraders and global share gains per IDC.
Mac revenue grew 29% to $10.4 billion despite significant supply constraints, driven by MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro, with all-time records for upgraders and customers new to Mac.
Supply constraints are driven by availability of advanced nodes for Apple's SoCs, which management attributed to demand exceeding forecasts rather than a supplier issue.
Memory costs rose significantly again in the June quarter and management expects even higher costs in September, prompting what Cook described as reluctant price increases on iPad and Mac.
Management described the response to Siri AI in developer and public betas as overwhelmingly positive, and said it will offer iCloud+ upgrade tiers for heavy users.
Services growth of 12% was pressured by FX, the prior-year F1 theatrical release, mobile gaming softness in the App Store, and App Store business model changes in certain countries.
Apple announced a multi-year agreement with Broadcom expected to exceed $30 billion as part of its American Manufacturing Program, its largest-ever such commitment.
Tim Cook confirmed this was his final earnings call, with John Ternus leading future calls.
financialHighlights: Total revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% year-over-year, a June quarter record.
Products revenue of $78.7 billion, up 18% year-over-year.
iPhone revenue of $54.3 billion, up 22% year-over-year.
Mac revenue of $10.4 billion, up 29% year-over-year.
iPad revenue of $6.2 billion, down 6% year-over-year on a difficult compare against the A16-powered iPad launch.
Wearables, home and accessories revenue of $7.9 billion, up 6% year-over-year.
Services revenue of $30.7 billion, up 12% year-over-year, with all-time records in cloud services and payment services.
Company gross margin of 50.1%, up 80 basis points sequentially, including approximately two percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

Products gross margin of 40.1%, up 140 basis points sequentially, including over 2.5 percentage points of tariff refund benefit; services gross margin of 75.6%, down 110 basis points sequentially on mix.
Operating expenses of $19.1 billion, up 23% year-over-year, driven by R&D investment.
Net income of $29.8 billion and diluted EPS of $2.02, up 29% year-over-year, including $0.11 of tariff refund benefit.
Operating cash flow of $34.4 billion.
Installed base of over 2.5 billion active devices and over 1.5 billion paid subscriptions.

Ended the quarter with $147 billion in cash and marketable securities and $84 billion in total debt; returned $33 billion to shareholders including $25.8 billion in buybacks and $4 billion in dividends.
Board declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share payable August 13, 2026.
guidance: Management expects September quarter total company revenue to grow 9%-11% year-over-year, assuming tariff policies remain as of the call and macro conditions do not worsen.
Management expects FX to be a sequential headwind of about 2.5 percentage points to the total company year-over-year growth rate from June to September.
Management expects the impact of supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad.
Management expects September quarter iPhone reported growth in the mid-teens year-over-year.

Management expects September quarter services growth to be largely similar to June after removing a roughly 2.5 percentage point sequential FX headwind, with FX a roughly 5 point headwind to services growth from March to September.
Management expects gross margin of 47%-48%, including approximately one percentage point of benefit from tariff refunds.
Management expects operating expenses of $19.1 billion-$19.4 billion, OI&E of around $350 million excluding mark-to-market of minority investments, and a tax rate of around 16.5%.

Management expects to pay even higher memory costs in September, partly offset by carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components, with carry-in benefit expected to decline beyond September.
Management declined to provide any color or guidance beyond the September quarter.
analystFocus: How much of the roughly 500 basis point sequential growth deceleration is supply constraint versus FX, and what the broadening constraints are.
Memory cost inflation, sourcing flexibility across the three DRAM suppliers, and possible multi-year LTAs with suppliers.
Pricing philosophy and whether Apple is protecting gross profit dollars or gross margin percentages after raising prices.
Whether supply constraints will extend into the December quarter and whether Apple could broaden its silicon providers.
Expected adoption of the new Apple Upgrade leasing program and its effect on replacement cycles.
Learnings from the iOS 27 and Siri AI public beta, its potential as a holiday iPhone demand driver, and compute cost recovery via iCloud+.
Drivers of services deceleration including App Store and mobile gaming softness.
Whether demand pull-forward has occurred ahead of price increases.
Whether Siri AI changes Apple's capital intensity given the hybrid first-party and third-party cloud model.
Rollout status of Siri AI in the EU and China.
Sequential gross margin drivers, with management attributing more than 100% of the decline to memory cost changes rather than FX.
risksMentioned: Supply constraints on advanced-node SoCs expected to increase significantly in the September quarter with limited supply chain flexibility.
Sharply rising memory costs, described by management as a 100-year flood, with market pricing expected to keep increasing beyond September and increasing potential business impact.
Foreign exchange headwinds to both total company and services growth.
Uncertain price elasticity following price increases on iPad and Mac.
Mobile gaming softness in the App Store and App Store business model changes in certain countries.
Ongoing U.S. court ruling impacting App Store link-out transactions, with a pending Supreme Court appeal.
Regulatory hurdles delaying Siri AI availability on iPhone and iPad in the European Union and additional work required for Siri AI approval in China.
Uncertain cost impact of Siri AI on OpEx and COGS versus iCloud+ monetization.
Tariffs, macroeconomic conditions, and legal and regulatory proceedings cited as forward-looking risk factors.
Tough year-over-year services compare from the prior-year F1 theatrical release affecting both June and September quarters.

parsed.overview: Chipotle's fiscal Q2 2026 call reported revenue growth of 9.3% to $3.3 billion with positive comparable sales and transactions, while management framed results around its Recipe for Growth strategy and noted softer trends in recent weeks.
keyTakeaways: Management reported comparable restaurant sales up 2.2% with transactions up 1%, supported by Chipotle Honey Chicken, Cilantro Lime Sauce, the rewards revamp and Summer of Extras.
Management said trends softened in the second half of July by about 200 basis points, linked to industry-wide Cyclospora concerns, and expects Q3 comps around plus 1%.
Management now expects full-year comp sales growth in the low single-digit range, up from the prior framing, and expects pricing near the high end of its 1%-2% range.

HEAP equipment is installed in more than 1,000 restaurants, with management still expecting approximately 2,000 by year-end and HEAP restaurants outperforming the enterprise by 2 to 3 entrees in the peak 15-minute period.

Management plans to open approximately 350 company-owned restaurants this year, with about 80% including a Chipotlane, and said it is preparing a national catering and Build-Your-Own family meal launch for 2027.
Management said only about 20% of in-restaurant transactions scan for rewards versus nearly 90% of own digital transactions, and plans a frictionless in-restaurant rewards pilot beginning in August.
Management said it repurchased $631 million of stock in Q2 at an average price of $32.55 and had $1.7 billion remaining on its authorization at quarter end.
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 9.3% to $3.3 billion in Q2.
Digital sales were $1.3 billion, or 38.3% of total sales, versus 35.5% in the prior year.
Restaurant level margin was 25.2%, down 220 basis points year-over-year.
Cost of sales was 29.7% of sales, up about 80 basis points year-over-year.
Labor costs were 25%, up about 30 basis points year-over-year.
Other operating costs were 14.9%, up about 90 basis points year-over-year.
Marketing costs were 3% of sales, up about 30 basis points year-over-year.
Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.33, flat year-over-year.
Non-GAAP G&A was $176 million in Q2, and depreciation was $98 million, or 2.9% of sales.
Cash, restricted cash and investments totalled $800 million at quarter end, with no debt and a $500 million revolver.
guidance: Management expects full-year comp sales growth in the low single-digit range and Q3 comps around plus 1%, assuming the roughly 200 basis point impact continues.
Management expects Q3 pricing to reach the mid 2% range, with full-year pricing near the high end of 1%-2%.
Management expects Q3 cost of sales just under 30% and cost of sales inflation in the low single-digit range.
Management expects Q3 labor costs in the mid 25% range and other operating costs in the mid 15% range.
Management expects marketing costs in the low 3% range for Q3 and for the full year.
Management expects Q3 non-GAAP G&A of around $180 million and depreciation around 3% of sales for 2026.
Management estimates a fiscal 2026 underlying effective tax rate of 24%-26%.
Management expects approximately 350 company-owned openings this year and approximately 2,000 HEAP restaurants by year-end.
Management expects the full HEAP portfolio to be completed sometime in 2027 and a Singapore opening in early 2027.
analystFocus: Analysts asked about the durability of comp growth into 2027 and the confidence behind the guidance raise.
Analysts probed the Q3 comp cadence and the Cyclospora-related softening in late July.
Questions covered limited-time offer lift, value perception, and whether protein offerings attract new or existing guests.
Analysts asked about remodel capital allocation, with management citing a $100,000-$300,000 per-restaurant test range and no results yet.
Questions addressed rewards enrollment in restaurants, digital sales growth, and the HEAP labor reinvestment.
Analysts asked about the 350-restaurant annual opening level, margin outlook as pricing and inflation converge, and performance by age and income cohort.
Analysts asked about the World Cup effect, which management said was less than five basis points for the quarter.
risksMentioned: Management cited heightened consumer caution around the broader restaurant industry and softer trends in recent weeks.
Management noted the Cyclospora industry issue affected sales by about 200 basis points in late July, with duration hard to predict.
Management noted Q3 comparisons are tougher due to increased promotional activity in the prior year.
Management said cost of sales inflation was driven by beef and freight, and that the gap between pricing and inflation was widest in the first half.
Management said near-term development in the Middle East depends on geopolitical conditions.
Management noted the risk of diminishing returns on repeated limited-time offers and possible fracturing of the base if openings grow too aggressively.

The company expanded its share buyback authorization by an additional $250 million, bringing total current authorization to $337 million.
Distribution and product expansion continued with 24 new wholesale broker appointments at Kinsale and 176 new retail broker appointments at Aspera so far this year.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating earnings per share increased by 15.9% to $5.54 per share for Q2 2026, compared to $4.78 per share in Q2 2025.

Gross written premium decreased by 5%, net written premium decreased by 1.4%, and net earned premium increased by 8.9% for the quarter.
The combined ratio for Q2 was 75.5%, including 4.5 points from net favorable prior year loss reserve development and 1.3 points from catastrophe losses.
Net income grew 31.1% and net operating earnings grew 13.3% quarter-over-quarter.
Net investment income increased by 19.9% in Q2, with float growing to $3.4 billion as of June 30, 2026.
Fixed maturity investment portfolio new money yields averaged around 5.25% with an average duration of 4.25 years.
guidance: Management expects year-over-year growth comparisons to become modestly easier in the third and fourth quarters of 2026 as property division comparisons ease.

analystFocus: Analysts asked about the drivers behind current accident year loss ratio performance and reserve conservatism.

Analysts questioned commercial property market trajectory and whether pricing declines are approaching a trough.
Analysts inquired about casualty loss trends, social inflation, and competition in long-tail lines.
risksMentioned: Management highlighted soft market conditions and material rate declines in Commercial Property driven by aggressive market competitors.

parsed.overview: Kinsale management reported fiscal Q2 2026 results marked by strong profitability despite a competitive E&S market, with gross written premium down 5% driven by a shrinking Commercial Property Division, while growth excluding that division was 3.7% for the quarter.
keyTakeaways: Management said diluted operating EPS rose 15.9% year over year and annualized operating ROE was 24.4% for the quarter.
Management said the Commercial Property Division faces material rate declines and expanding coverage, and that it is writing a shrinking volume of business there.
Management said it prioritises profitability over growth, and that it will not sacrifice profitability for top-line growth.
Management said the company expects its share repurchase authorisation expansion of an additional $250 million to bring the total authorisation to $337 million.
Management said new product rollouts and broker appointments are supporting submissions, with growth expected to be slow until market conditions turn.
financialHighlights: Gross written premium was down 5% for the quarter; net written premium was down 1.4%; net earned premium was up 8.9%.
Combined ratio was 75.5% for the quarter, including 4.5 points of net favourable prior year reserve development versus 3.9 points last year.
Catastrophe losses were 1.3 points this year versus less than one point in Q2 2025.
Expense ratio was 21.7% versus 20.7% last year; other underwriting expense ratio was 10.3% versus 10.6%.
Net income increased 31.1% and net operating earnings increased 13.3% quarter over quarter, per management's comments.
Net investment income rose 19.9% year over year; float grew to $3.4 billion at June 30 from $3.1 billion at end of 2025.
Annualized gross investment return was 4.5% for the first half of 2026 versus 4.3% last year; new money yields averaged around 5.25% with average duration of 4.25 years.
Diluted operating EPS was $5.54 for the quarter versus $4.78 in Q2 2025.

parsed.overview: Lilly reported fiscal Q2 2026 revenue growth of 48% versus Q2 2025, led by ZEPBOUND and MOUNJARO, and raised its full-year revenue and EPS guidance. Management also discussed the Foundayo launch, the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program, positive retatrutide phase III results, and several business development deals.
keyTakeaways: Revenue grew 48% year over year, and key products increased by almost $6.8 billion.
Oncology, immunology and neuroscience medicines collectively grew 121% versus Q2 2025.
MOUNJARO and ZEPBOUND combined for $14.9 billion of revenue, contributing $6.3 billion of growth versus Q2 2025.
Management said Foundayo is seeing an inflection, with volume almost doubling versus a month earlier and about one in four new starts in the last week of July.

The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program launched July 1, granting 20 million eligible Americans coverage for obesity GLP-1s at $50 per month, which management said means 35% more people have coverage for its obesity medicines.
Positive top-line results came from three retatrutide phase III trials (TRIUMPH-1, -2 and -3), and management plans a U.S. BLA submission in Q1 2027.
Lilly announced acquisitions including Curevo, LimmaTech Biologics, The Vaccine Company and AtaiBeckley, and completed the Centessa acquisition.
Lilly's share of the international incretin market rose almost 2 percentage points versus Q1 2026 to about 55%.
financialHighlights: Gross margin was 86.3% of revenue, up approximately 1.3 percentage points year over year, on favorable product mix and improved cost of production.
Marketing, selling and administrative expenses rose 25% and R&D expenses rose 14%, with more than 40 active phase III programs.
Non-GAAP performance margin was 54.8%, up nine percentage points from Q2 2025.
Non-GAAP EPS was $8.38, including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges, versus $6.31 in Q2 2025, which included $0.14 of such charges.
U.S. revenue grew 33%, and U.S. price declined 3% (9% excluding a favorable change to rebate and discount estimates).
Europe revenue grew 55% in constant currency and included a $250 million Jardiance milestone payment.
Japan revenue grew 30%, China 93% and rest of world 136%, all in constant currency.
Ebglyss worldwide sales more than doubled, Jaypirca sales rose 56%, and INLURIYO holds over 50% of U.S. new prescriptions in the oral SERD market.
U.S. incretin analog total prescriptions grew 31%, and within obesity they grew 78%, with roughly six in 10 total prescriptions for a Lilly medicine.
Self-pay accounted for about 45% of total ZEPBOUND prescriptions and about 55% of new prescriptions.
Lilly paid $1.5 billion in dividends and executed $1.6 billion of share repurchases in the quarter.
In Q&A an analyst cited Q2 Foundayo sales of $31 million in the UAE and $67 million in the U.S.; management did not dispute these figures.
guidance: Management now expects full-year 2026 revenue of $85 billion to $87 billion, raising the low end by $3 billion and the high end by $2 billion.
Management expects non-GAAP performance margin of 49% to 50.5%, up 2 percentage points at both ends of the range.
Management expects non-GAAP EPS of $35.50 to $36.50, an increase of $2.78 per share at the midpoint before the $3.03 Q2 acquired IPR&D charge impact.
Management said the guide factors in Q3 European seasonality, Q4 U.S. Type 2 diabetes seasonality, and no repeat of the prior-period rebate and discount adjustments.
Management expects a global Foundayo rollout in all major markets in 2027 and regulatory action on the U.S. Type 2 diabetes submission later this year.
Management expects more than 40 additional countries to review Foundayo, with additional approvals later this year, and the first obstructive sleep apnea readout later this year.
Management plans a U.S. retatrutide BLA submission in Q1 2027 and said it still needs to gather more CMC data.
Management expects the EMBER-4 adjuvant readout next year and lebrikizumab every-12-week dosing data in 2027.
Management expects ZEPBOUND and MOUNJARO net price to fall as CVS access returns beginning in Q4, saying this is embedded in guidance and will be more than offset by volume growth.
analystFocus: Consumer and self-pay market expansion in the U.S. and internationally.
Pace of the U.S. Foundayo launch, the inflection timing, and competition from Novo Nordisk's oral launch outside the U.S.
Retatrutide BLA regulatory pathway and litigation with the FDA.
Early learnings from the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge rollout and the oral versus injectable mix.
Retatrutide commercial strategy against unauthorized supply and additional indications.
Post-Verzenio breast cancer strategy and all-oral combinations.
Whether second-half guidance implies a revenue deceleration.
Ex-U.S. MOUNJARO growth and the impact of generic semaglutide in India and other markets.
Foundayo sampling, prescriber base and its effect on prescription data.
Net pricing in obesity, medical exceptions, and rebate adjustments.
Strategy behind psychiatry and vaccine acquisitions, and non-obesity pipeline highlights.
Foundayo ex-U.S. obesity potential and Type 2 diabetes reimbursement.
risksMentioned: Retatrutide BLA classification is subject to active litigation with the FDA, and the CMC data package is still being completed.
U.S. net price pressure, including medical exception dynamics, and the fact that Q2 benefited from non-recurring rebate estimate changes.
Generic semaglutide launches outside the U.S., although management noted generic suppliers face supply constraints.
Competition from a second oral GLP-1 entering ex-U.S. markets such as the UAE.
Ex-U.S. reimbursement timelines that management said always take time.
Seasonality in Europe in Q3 and U.S. Type 2 diabetes in Q4.
Unauthorized or non-authentic retatrutide available in the market.
Management cautioned that early Foundayo ex-U.S. data is noisy and affected by inventory build.

parsed.overview: JPMorgan Chase reported Q2 2026 net income of $16.9 billion, EPS of $6.14 and ROTCE of 23%, with revenue (ex-significant items) up 15% year-on-year driven by markets, asset management fees, investment banking and balance growth; management raised full-year NII and expense guidance and lowered the card net charge-off outlook, while Q&A focused on succession, operating leverage, capital deployment, AI, regulation and the sustainability of capital markets strength.
keyTakeaways: Equities markets revenue rose 86% year-on-year, which CFO Jeremy Barnum said reflected an unusual combination of events that seems statistically improbable to repeat.
IB fees rose 30% year-on-year with some pull-forward and large deals, but management described the pipeline as quite robust.
Management raised full-year NII ex-Markets guidance from $95 billion to about $96.5 billion, mainly on deposit balances.
Adjusted expense guidance was raised by $2.5 billion to about $107.5 billion, primarily on volume- and revenue-related expenses.
Jamie Dimon said the elevation of two co-presidents has not changed the CEO succession timetable, which he described as 'several years' and up to the board.
Dimon said the environment is 'getting close to as good as it gets' but that management does not know how long it will last.
Management said its priority is deploying excess capital organically at a targeted 17% return, while staying open to inorganic opportunities.
financialHighlights: Net income was $16.9 billion, EPS $6.14 and ROTCE 23%, including significant items.
Expenses were $27.3 billion, up 15% year-on-year.
Credit costs were $2.5 billion, with net charge-offs of $2.4 billion and a net reserve build of $149 million.
Standardized CET1 ratio was 14.1%, down 20 basis points quarter-on-quarter, as standardized RWA rose about $103 billion.
The board intends to raise the quarterly dividend to $1.65 per share effective Q3.
CCB net income was $5.3 billion on revenue of $20.3 billion, up 8% year-on-year.
CCB average deposits rose 3% year-on-year and 2% quarter-on-quarter, with over 500,000 net new checking accounts, and client investment assets rose 21% year-on-year.
CIB net income was $9.7 billion on revenue of $24.9 billion, up 27% year-on-year.
Fixed income markets revenue rose 6% year-on-year, while equities rose 86%.
AWM net income was $2 billion on revenue of $6.9 billion, up 19% year-on-year, with a 38% pre-tax margin.
AWM long-term net inflows were $50 billion, AUM was $5.1 trillion (up 18%) and client assets were $7.7 trillion (up 19%).
Corporate net income was $4.2 billion on revenue of $6 billion, including significant items.
First-half capital markets revenue beat prior expectations by $6.5 billion, with $1.5 billion of associated additional expense booked.
guidance: Management expects full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets of about $96.5 billion and total NII of about $105.5 billion, with markets NII of about $9 billion.
Management expects full-year adjusted expenses of about $107.5 billion, including an implied extra $1 billion in the second half.
Management expects a card net charge-off rate of approximately 3.2%, citing better-than-expected consumer credit.
Management continues to expect low single-digit consumer deposit growth this year.
Management implied a higher NII exit run rate, assuming the yield curve follows forwards.
Management expects investment banking activity levels to remain healthy, subject to market conditions.
About $150 million of the markets NII increase stems from higher equity allocation to the CIB, which management does not expect to be offset in NIR.
Dimon said expense growth could slow in 2027 or 2028.
Dimon said a smart cash tool test should appear this year.
Barnum said token (AI usage) expense is expected to accelerate in the second half but remain trivial for the full year.
analystFocus: CEO succession, the co-president appointments, Marianne's departure and Troy's suitability to run the consumer bank.
Sustainability of investment banking and markets strength, including pull-forward effects and what drove equities.
Drivers of the NII ex-Markets and markets NII revisions, including rates, deposit balances and balance sheet mix.
Operating leverage, expense growth and returns on investment in branches, bankers and AI.
Deposit market share progress toward 15% retail share and deposit beta and convexity risk if rates rise.
Regulatory proposals, including G-SIB surcharge, Basel III, short-term wholesale funding and prospects for regulatory stability.
Consumer health, the K-shape narrative and whether CapEx is broadening beyond AI.
Buybacks at current valuations versus organic deployment and M&A, plus European digital consumer banking ambitions.
Credit underwriting standards among competitors, particularly in data centers.
AI efficiency potential, token costs and CIB capital allocation limits.
risksMentioned: Yield-seeking deposit flows in a more hawkish rate environment were described as a risk.
Negative convexity in consumer deposit pricing could eventually trigger an accelerated rise in rates paid if rates climb sharply.
Elevated gas prices, inflation and negative real wage growth for some consumer cohorts were flagged as a watch area.
Management said consumer credit performance ultimately depends on the labor market.
Management cited a mild weakening in industry credit standards, including revenue assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants and rollover risk.
Dimon warned that some outliers will perform poorly in an eventual credit cycle.
Data center lending carries power supply and tenant risks, and the firm passed on some deals.
Barnum said the market is extremely risk-on, with complicated dynamics.
Regulatory proposals, especially the short-term wholesale funding change, could disproportionately burden universal banks.
Barnum said the system is less flush with liquidity at the margin.
Management cited competition from Goldman Sachs and fintechs including Stripe, PayPal, Cash App, Block, Chime, SoFi and Revolut.
Chase's German digital operations are not yet profitable.

parsed.overview: Deere & Company reported its fiscal Q3 2026 financial results, highlighted by 6% growth in equipment operations net sales to $10.999 billion and an equipment operations operating margin of 14.4%, leading management to raise full-year net income and cash flow guidance.
keyTakeaways: Management believes fiscal year 2026 represents the trough of the agricultural equipment cycle, supported by early order programs for planters and sprayers that are up mid-single digits year-over-year.
Production & Precision Ag order books are closed for the fiscal year, with management intentionally underproducing retail demand in South America to maintain healthy channel inventory.
Construction & Forestry order backlogs now extend into fiscal 2027, driven by strong demand in infrastructure, data center, and energy projects.
Adoption of precision technologies continues to grow, with factory installation of See & Spray expected to nearly double on model year 2027 sprayer orders.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues increased 5% year-over-year to $12.608 billion, while equipment operations net sales reached $10.999 billion.
Net income attributable to Deere & Company for the quarter was $1.379 billion, or $5.10 per diluted share.
Production & Precision Ag net sales declined 6% year-over-year to $3.998 billion, with an operating profit of $527 million and a 13.2% operating margin.
Small Ag & Turf net sales rose 12% year-over-year to $3.383 billion, generating an operating profit of $622 million and an 18.4% operating margin.
Construction & Forestry net sales surged 18% year-over-year to $3.618 billion, producing an operating profit of $436 million and a 12.1% operating margin.
Financial Services recorded net income attributable to Deere & Company of $219 million for the third quarter.
guidance: Management raised its fiscal 2026 net income outlook to a range of $4.75 billion to $5.0 billion.
Equipment operations cash flow for fiscal 2026 was upgraded to a range of $5.0 billion to $5.5 billion.
Management expects Production & Precision Ag full-year net sales to decline approximately 10%, with segment operating margin narrowed to between 11% and 12%.
Small Ag & Turf full-year net sales are projected to increase approximately 15%, with the operating margin outlook increased to between 14.5% and 15.5%.
Construction & Forestry full-year net sales are expected to grow approximately 20%, with segment operating margin projected between 10.5% and 11.5%.
Management raised the full-year net income forecast for Financial Services to $870 million while maintaining an effective tax rate guide between 24% and 26%.
analystFocus: Analysts focused on early order program progress, regional order intake variance, and pricing dynamics entering model year 2027.
Questions addressed net tariff impacts, including direct expenses, section policy updates, and recognized refunds.
Analysts sought clarity on production-versus-retail inventory alignment across major international regions.
Analysts inquired about market reception for Deere-designed excavators and expansion of dealer rental fleets.
risksMentioned: Management cited ongoing pressure on farm profitability due to elevated input costs, high interest rates, and commodity price volatility in regions like South America and Europe.
Direct tariff expense is expected to total approximately $1.1 billion in fiscal 2026, representing a net cost headwind entering fiscal 2027.
Global forestry demand remains constrained due to sluggish residential construction activity and weak lumber prices.

parsed.overview: Deere's fiscal Q3 2026 call reported net sales and revenues up 5% to $12.608 billion and equipment operations margin of 14.4%, with management narrowing or raising several FY2026 guidance items and describing 2026 as the bottom of the ag equipment cycle.
keyTakeaways: Management reported Q3 net income attributable to Deere of $1.379 billion, or $5.10 per diluted share.
Management raised FY2026 net income guidance to $4.75 billion-$5 billion and equipment operations cash flow guidance to $5 billion-$5.5 billion.
Management now expects Production & Precision Ag net sales to be down approximately 10% for the year, with operating margin of 11%-12%.
Management expects Small Ag & Turf operating margin of 14.5%-15.5% with net sales up approximately 15%.
Management expects Construction & Forestry net sales up approximately 20% for the year, with operating margin of 10.5%-11.5%.
Management believes 2026 represents the bottom of the agricultural equipment cycle, with a measured recovery expected in 2027.
Management expects FY2026 direct tariff expense of approximately $1.1 billion excluding IEPA refunds, with total refunds recognized of $382 million.
Management said early order programs for planters and sprayers are running up mid-single digits compared with last year's completed programs.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues rose 5% to $12.608 billion; equipment operations net sales rose 6% to $10.999 billion.
Production & Precision Ag Q3 net sales were $3.998 billion, down 6%, with operating profit of $527 million and a 13.2% operating margin.
Small Ag & Turf Q3 net sales rose 12% to $3.383 billion, with operating profit of $622 million and an 18.4% operating margin.
Construction & Forestry Q3 net sales rose 18% to $3.618 billion, with price realization of positive 8 points and operating profit of $436 million, a 12.1% margin.
Worldwide Financial Services Q3 net income attributable to Deere was $219 million; FY2026 outlook increased to $870 million.
Management recognized $110 million of incremental tariff refunds in Q3, and FY2026 refunds total $382 million.
Management expects an effective tax rate between 24% and 26% for FY2026.
Management expects direct tariff expense of about $1.1 billion for FY2026, down from a previously communicated run rate of $1.2 billion, mainly due to Section 232 changes.
guidance: Management expects PPA price realization of one point and currency translation of close to 2.5 points for FY2026.
Management expects Small Ag & Turf price realization of 1.5 points and currency translation of roughly half a point for FY2026.
Management expects Construction & Forestry price realization of 3 points and currency translation of approximately 1.5 points for FY2026.
Management expects U.S. and Canada large ag equipment industry sales to decline 15%-20% in 2026.
Management expects South America industry outlook to be down 15%-20% for 2026.
Management expects Europe industry sales to be approximately flat for 2026.
Management expects U.S. and Canada construction equipment industry sales to be up 5%-10% and compact construction up 5% in 2026.
Management expects global forestry industry sales to be down 10% and global road building up approximately 10% in 2026.
Management expects net tariff expense of roughly $1 billion for FY2027, a step up from the approximately $750 million net exposure in FY2026.
Management expects a Q4 net sales level for PPA and C&F similar to Q3, with lower margins for PPA and Small Ag & Turf due to seasonal R&D and SA&G costs.
analystFocus: Analysts asked about 2027 production versus retail by region and pricing expectations, with management citing modest underproduction of about a couple of percentage points in PPA and C&F.
Analysts questioned the drop in expected tariff expense to $1.1 billion, with management attributing it to Section 232 rate changes from about 25% to 15% effective 1 June.
Analysts asked about the excavator launch, with management stating three models are in market and more will roll out over three to four years.
Analysts questioned inventory build in Q3 tractors, with management saying shipment plans are set and inventory is on trend with historical averages.
Analysts asked about mix benefits from technology adoption, with management saying it is too early to tell for 2027.
Analysts asked about early order program variability by region, with management saying the U.S. is trending slightly better than Canada.
Analysts asked about C&F order books and rental fleet exposure, with management citing four to five months of orders and rentals at 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions.
Analysts asked about European demand and the 2028 policy change, with management saying it is too early to tell.
risksMentioned: Management cited muted farm profitability, elevated input costs, and commodity price volatility as pressures on ag equipment demand.
Management cited elevated production costs, fertilizer expenses, and higher interest rates weighing on South American farm economics.
Management cited heat and drought, elevated input costs, and crop economics pressuring European arable farm profitability.
Management cited tariffs and shipment disruptions, including Black Sea issues, as uncertainties affecting agriculture.
Management cited subdued residential construction and softer log and lumber prices weighing on forestry equipment demand.
Management cautioned that Brazil and European softness could affect 2027 mix, and that South American conditions can turn quickly.
Management noted that C&F order books at four to five months are more than it would want to have.

parsed.overview: Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG) reported strong Q2 2026 results driven by positive transaction growth and the successful execution of its Recipe for Growth strategy.
keyTakeaways: Management highlighted the successful return of Chipotle Honey Chicken and continued strength from Cilantro Lime sauce.
The company relaunched its Chipotle Rewards program in mid-April to increase personalization and deepen guest engagement.
Management noted that the High-Efficiency Equipment Package (HEAP) is now installed in over 1,000 restaurants and is expected to reach approximately 2,000 by year-end.
The company opened 101 new restaurants in the quarter, including 80 Chipotlanes.
Management expects to open approximately 350 restaurants this year, with about 80% including a Chipotlane.
The company is preparing for a national launch of its catering and Build-Your-Own Chipotle options in 2027.
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 9.3% to $3.3 billion in the second quarter.
Comparable restaurant sales increased 2.2%, including a transaction comp of 1%.
Digital sales were $1.3 billion, representing 38.3% of total sales.
Restaurant level margin was 25.2%, down 220 basis points year-over-year.
Adjusted diluted earnings per share was $0.33, flat to last year.
Cost of sales in the quarter were 29.7%, an increase of about 80 basis points from last year.
Labor costs for the quarter were 25%, an increase of about 30 basis points from last year.
The company repurchased $631 million of stock in the second quarter at an average price of $32.55.
guidance: Management expects full-year comp sales growth in the low single-digit range.
Management anticipates Q3 cost of sales to be just under 30%.
Management expects Q3 labor costs to be in the mid 25% range.
Management expects Q3 marketing costs to remain in the low 3% range, and for the full year, also in the low 3% range.
Management anticipates Q3 other operating costs to be in the mid 15% range.
Management expects Q3 non-GAAP G&A to be around $180 million.
Management expects 2026 depreciation to remain around 3% of sales.
Management estimates the underlying effective tax rate for fiscal 2026 will be in the 24%-26% range.
analystFocus: Analysts asked about the impact of returning limited-time offerings (LTOs) and value perception.
Questions were raised regarding the company's confidence in picking up momentum into 2027 despite recent industry challenges.
Analysts inquired about the specific impact of the Cyclospora issue on recent sales trends.
Questions were asked about capital allocation, specifically regarding store refreshes and international partnerships.
Analysts sought clarification on the drivers of digital sales growth and the impact of loyalty program changes.
Questions were raised about the expected benefits of the HEAP rollout on labor efficiency and throughput.
risksMentioned: Management noted that trends have been softer in recent weeks amid heightened consumer caution around the broader restaurant industry.
Management mentioned a roughly 200 basis point impact on sales in the second half of July related to an industry-wide Cyclospora issue, though Chipotle is not directly involved.
Management highlighted that cost of sales inflation was driven primarily by beef and freight, as well as increased usage of several ingredients.
Management noted that labor costs increased due to wage inflation and performance bonuses.
