parsed.overview: Chipotle reported fiscal Q2 2026 revenue growth of 9.3% to $3.3 billion, with comparable sales up 2.2% and transactions up 1%, which management attributed to its Recipe for Growth strategy, menu innovation and the rewards relaunch. Management raised full-year comp guidance to the low single-digit range while noting softer trends in late July tied to industry Cyclospora concerns and a tougher Q3 comparison.
keyTakeaways: Management said Recipe for Growth initiatives are gaining traction, citing the return of Chipotle Honey Chicken (cumulative attachment rate north of 25%), Cilantro Lime Sauce, the rewards relaunch and marketing activations.
Linebacker was deployed in over 70% of restaurants for the first time, and year-over-year Max 15 performance accelerated for the second quarter in a row.

HEAP equipment is in more than 1,000 restaurants, with management still expecting about 2,000 by year-end and the full portfolio sometime in 2027; HEAP restaurants outperform the enterprise by 2 to 3 entrees in the peak 15 minutes.

Chipotle Rewards has 23 million active members; only about 20% of in-restaurant transactions scan for rewards versus nearly 90% of own digital transactions, and a frictionless in-restaurant pilot is planned to begin in August.
Catering and Build-Your-Own Chipotle represent 2%-3% of sales, and management is positioning for a national catering launch in 2027.
Management said the younger and lower-income cohorts improved the most, and that Chipotle has taken share in each month of 2026.
Management stated it opened 100 company-owned restaurants in the quarter, entered Monterrey, Mexico, and plans Seoul openings this year and Singapore in early 2027.
Management said Cyclospora does not involve Chipotle's products, but the industry issue has affected its sales.
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 9.3% to $3.3 billion; comparable restaurant sales rose 2.2%, including a 1% transaction comp.
Digital sales were $1.3 billion, or 38.3% of total sales versus 35.5% a year earlier.
Restaurant level margin was 25.2%, down 220 basis points year over year.
Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.33, flat versus last year.
Cost of sales were 29.7% (up about 80 bps), labor 25% (up about 30 bps), and other operating costs 14.9% (up about 90 bps); marketing was 3% of sales.
Non-GAAP G&A was $176 million (GAAP $190 million); depreciation was $98 million, or 2.9% of sales.
Effective tax rate was 24.3% GAAP and 24.0% non-GAAP.
The company opened 101 new restaurants, including 80 Chipotlanes and one international partner-operated restaurant.
Cash, restricted cash and investments were $800 million, with no debt; Q2 buybacks were $631 million at an average $32.55, over $1.3 billion year to date at an average $34.35.
The board added $1.3 billion to the repurchase authorization, leaving $1.7 billion remaining.
guidance: Management now expects full-year comp sales growth in the low single-digit range.
Management expects Q3 comps of around plus 1%, assuming the roughly 200 basis point late-July softness continues.
Management expects Q3 pricing impact in the mid 2% range, up from about 1.6% in Q2, and full-year pricing near the high end of the 1%-2% range.
Management expects Q3 cost of sales just under 30% with low single-digit inflation, labor in the mid 25% range, and other operating costs in the mid 15% range.
Management expects marketing in the low 3% range for Q3 and the full year.
Management expects Q3 non-GAAP G&A of around $180 million, depreciation around 3% of sales for 2026, and an underlying tax rate of 24%-26%.
Management still expects about 350 company-owned openings in 2026, about 80% with a Chipotlane.
Management expects pricing and inflation to match from Q4 onward.
analystFocus: Analysts asked about LTO lift over repeat launches and value perception, and management said Honey Chicken performed better the second time but returns may diminish after several repeats.
Analysts probed confidence in momentum into 2027 and the low single-digit comp guide, including the softening in late July.
Analysts asked about the Q3 comp guide, with confirmation that it embeds roughly a 200 basis point Cyclospora-related headwind.
Questions covered the restaurant remodel program, which management is testing at $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant with no results yet.
Analysts asked about the 350-opening pace versus a prior 400 ceiling and the role of partner-operated markets.
Analysts asked about digital and loyalty drivers, HEAP labor reinvestment and Max 15 throughput levels, and in-restaurant rewards enrollment.

Questions addressed brand evolution under the new Chief Brand Officer, upcoming menu innovation, margin and pricing versus inflation, World Cup impact (under 5 bps for the quarter), and pricing strategy.
risksMentioned: Management cited softer trends in recent weeks amid heightened consumer caution around the restaurant industry and the industry Cyclospora issue, and said it is hard to predict how long the impact will last.
Management noted Q3 is the toughest comparison of the year because it laps increased promotional activity in the prior year.
Cost pressures included beef and freight inflation, higher ingredient usage, wage inflation, and higher insurance, maintenance and utility costs.
Management said near-term Middle East development depends on geopolitical conditions.
Management noted potential diminishing returns from repeated LTOs and from opening beyond 350 restaurants per year.
Management said the remodel return is unproven and the results are still to be determined.

parsed.overview: Kinsale reported Q2 2026 diluted operating EPS of $5.54, up 15.9% year over year, with an annualized operating ROE of 24.4% and a 75.5% combined ratio, while gross written premium fell 5% amid intense competition in the Commercial Property Division.
keyTakeaways: Management said E&S conditions were competitive and largely consistent with Q1, with the Commercial Property Division facing the most intense competition, material rate declines and expanding coverage.
Excluding the Commercial Property Division, gross written premium grew 3.7% in the quarter and 4.8% in the first half.

Management said it prioritizes profitability over growth and will not chase soft markets, while leaning into areas such as excess casualty, commercial auto, Entertainment, Environmental, Agribusiness Casualty and Energy.
New business submissions rose 6% overall and 8% excluding the Commercial Property Division, with over half of divisions seeing double-digit submission growth.
Management described its reserves as as conservative as they have ever been, and said it is slowing IBNR releases in longer-tail lines while releasing more in short-tail lines.
The board expanded the buyback authorization by $250 million to $337 million, which management called its principal capital allocation strategy.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS was $5.54 versus $4.78 in Q2 2025, up 15.9%.
Annualized operating ROE was 24.4%.
Gross written premium was down 5%, net written premium down 1.4%, and net earned premium up 8.9%.
Net income rose 31.1% and net operating earnings rose 13.3% year over year.
Combined ratio was 75.5%, including 4.5 points of favorable prior year reserve development (3.9 points last year) and 1.3 points of cat losses.

Expense ratio was 21.7% versus 20.7% last year, with the other underwriting expense ratio at 10.3% versus 10.6%; the increase reflected a higher net commission ratio from higher reinsurance retentions.
Net investment income rose 19.9%, and float grew to $3.4 billion at June 30 from $3.1 billion at year-end 2025.
Annualized gross investment return was 4.5% for the first half of 2026 versus 4.3% last year, with new money yields around 5.25% and fixed maturity duration of about 4.25 years.
guidance: Management said Q2's expense ratio should be a good measure going forward, with a possible slight uptick in commissions after the June 1 reinsurance renewals, potentially offset by AI-driven efficiency gains.

Management noted that 60% of Commercial Property Division premium was written in the first half of last year, so year-over-year growth comparisons become modestly easier in the next two quarters of 2026.
Management said the current accident year loss ratio could drift up over time given mix shift, though losses have come in below expectations.
Management said it will continue to lean into buybacks while growth is limited, and would prioritize growth if it accelerates.
Management said new products will grow slowly at a crawl, walk, run pace, with five more launches imminent and 10 in the pipeline.
analystFocus: Drivers of the improved current accident year loss ratio, and whether it is sustainable given mix shift from property to casualty.
Reinsurance ceding commission trends after renewals.
Whether Commercial Property pricing and volume have troughed, and where property pricing stabilizes.
Broker commission pressure and flow of business to the admitted market.
Sources of inbound submission growth, and views on social inflation and casualty loss trends.
Buyback pacing and the contribution of new products to growth.
risksMentioned: Intense competition and rate declines in Commercial Property, with competitors underpricing risk and MGAs and London markets adding pressure.
Softening in Construction, certain Professional Lines and general casualty, with London competition creeping into long-tail liability lines.
Pricing index showed a 5.9% decrease versus a 3.3% decrease in Q1 2026.
Tension with brokers over commissions in a soft market, and some business flowing to the admitted market.
Casualty loss cost trends in the mid-single digits, and unpredictable catastrophe losses.

parsed.overview: JPMorgan Chase reported fiscal Q2 2026 net income of $16.9 billion, EPS of $6.14 and ROTCE of 23%, with revenue excluding significant items up 15% year-on-year on markets, asset management fees, investment banking and higher deposit and loan balances; management raised full-year NII and expense guidance, lowered the card net charge-off outlook, and fielded extensive questions on succession, operating leverage, AI, capital deployment and regulation.
keyTakeaways: Revenue excluding significant items rose 15% year-on-year, driven predominantly by markets revenue, higher asset management fees in AWM and CCB, higher investment banking revenue and higher deposit and loan balances, partially offset by lower rates.

CIB net income was $9.7 billion on revenue of $24.9 billion (up 27% year-on-year), with IB fees up 30% and equities revenue up 86% year-on-year, which management described as an exceptionally strong quarter unlikely to be repeated in that exact combination.

Management raised full-year 2026 guidance for NII ex-Markets to about $96.5 billion, total NII to approximately $105.5 billion, and adjusted expense to about $107.5 billion, while lowering the expected card net charge-off rate to approximately 3.2%.

Jamie Dimon said the elevation of two co-presidents and Marianne Lake's departure did not change the CEO succession timetable, which he described as 'several years, plus or minus' and up to the board.
Dimon characterised the current environment as 'getting close to as good as it gets' with very high prices and volumes, adding that management does not know how long it will last.

Management reiterated it is always investing, said operating leverage is positive in dollar terms, and Dimon suggested expense growth could slow in 2027 or 2028 while cautioning that AI benefits ultimately accrue to customers rather than margins.

Management said excess capital of approximately $40 billion is expected to be deployed over time, prefers organic growth at a 17% return target, remains open to inorganic opportunities, and intends to buy back less stock as the price rises.
financialHighlights: Net income of $16.9 billion, EPS of $6.14, and ROTCE of 23%, including significant items.
Expenses of $27.3 billion, up 15% year-on-year, driven by volume and revenue-related expense, front office hiring and labor inflation.
Credit costs of $2.5 billion, comprising net charge-offs of $2.4 billion and a net reserve build of $149 million.
Standardized CET1 ratio of 14.1%, down 20 basis points quarter-on-quarter, with standardized RWA up approximately $103 billion on markets financing and traditional lending growth.

CCB net income of $5.3 billion on revenue of $20.3 billion (up 8% year-on-year), with average deposits up 3% year-on-year, net new checking accounts of over 500,000, and client investment assets up 21% year-on-year.
CIB net income of $9.7 billion on revenue of $24.9 billion (up 27% year-on-year); IB fees up 30%, fixed income up 6%, and equities up 86% year-on-year.

AWM net income of $2 billion with a 38% pre-tax margin on revenue of $6.9 billion (up 19% year-on-year); long-term net inflows of $50 billion, AUM of $5.1 trillion (up 18%) and client assets of $7.7 trillion (up 19%).
Corporate net income of $4.2 billion on revenue of $6 billion, including significant items.
Management said the capital markets complex outperformed prior expectations by $6.5 billion in the first half, with $1.5 billion of associated additional expenses booked.
guidance: Management now expects full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets of about $96.5 billion (up from $95 billion), driven mainly by higher deposit balances and mix, with some contribution from higher rates, implying a higher exit run rate in the central case.

Management expects total NII of approximately $105.5 billion, with markets NII increasing to about $9 billion, reflecting balance sheet composition changes and an equity allocation shift of roughly $150 million of NII into the CIB.

Management's adjusted expense outlook is about $107.5 billion, raised by $2.5 billion, of which $1.5 billion is already booked volume and revenue-related expense and roughly $1 billion is implicitly added for the second half.
Management now expects the card net charge-off rate to be approximately 3.2%, reflecting better-than-expected consumer credit performance.
The board intends to increase the quarterly dividend to $1.65 per share effective in the third quarter.
Management continues to expect low single-digit consumer deposit growth for the year and said wholesale deposit growth has outperformed expectations in the first half.

Management expects investment banking activity levels to remain healthy given a robust pipeline, with conversion dependent on market conditions, while cautioning there was some pull-forward this quarter.
Management said a 'smart cash' deposit tool test will be rolled out to a narrow segment of accounts this year.
Dimon indicated expense growth might slow in 2027 or 2028, and management expects a meaningful acceleration in AI token expense in the second half, though the full-year amount remains trivial.
analystFocus: Succession planning following the appointment of co-presidents and Marianne Lake's departure, including Dimon's tenure and Troy's suitability to run the consumer bank.
Sustainability of investment banking and markets strength, and what was exceptional in equities this quarter.
Negative operating leverage year-to-date, the $2.5 billion expense guidance increase, and whether AI could slow expense growth.
Drivers and cadence of the upward NII ex-Markets revision and the markets NII increase.
Deposit growth, progress toward 15% retail deposit share, and whether higher rates could change deposit betas or volumes.
Capital deployment including buybacks at three times tangible book, potential M&A, and increased capital allocation to the CIB.
Regulatory outlook including Basel III, G-SIB surcharge, short-term wholesale funding treatment and prospects for regulatory stability.
Main Street consumer health, housing fragility, breadth of CapEx beyond AI, and competitor credit underwriting standards.
AI efficiency potential, token expense, European digital banking aspirations and the smart cash tool.
risksMentioned: Management said the equities performance this quarter reflected a combination of IPOs, index rebalancing, Korean equity market dynamics and Asia activity that is statistically improbable to repeat.
Some investment banking revenue was pulled forward and boosted by large ECM deals, with conversion of the pipeline dependent on market conditions.
Yield-seeking deposit flows remain a factor and 'a little bit of a risk' in a more hawkish rate environment.

Management warned not to be naïve about higher rates, noting negative convexity in deposit rate paid could kick in and a 7% rate environment would not be benign if a large repricing of the deposit franchise were required.
Dimon described the market as exuberant with very high prices and volumes and said management does not know how long it will last.
Elevated gas prices and inflation, and a cohort of consumers with negative real wage growth, were flagged as watch areas, with consumer credit ultimately tied to the labor market.

Management noted mild deterioration in competitor credit underwriting (aggressive revenue assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants, rollover risk) and said JPMorgan passed on some data center deals over power and tenant risk.
Dimon said a credit cycle will come and performance across lenders is unlikely to be a bell curve, with some outliers.

Regulatory issues cited include double counting in operational and market risk capital, G-SIB calibration, and short-term wholesale funding treatment that management said disproportionately burdens banks with both markets and consumer businesses.
Management noted the system is flush with capital but less so with liquidity, and reducing the Fed balance sheet may require adjustments to liquidity regulation.
Intense competition from Goldman Sachs and fintechs such as Stripe, PayPal, Cash App, Block, Chime, SoFi and Revolut requires ongoing investment.
Management said AI benefits will ultimately accrue to customers rather than durably higher margins, and AI token expense is expected to accelerate.

parsed.overview: Eli Lilly reported Q2 2026 revenue growth of 48% year over year, driven by MOUNJARO and ZEPBOUND (combined $14.9 billion), with oncology, immunology and neuroscience key products growing 121% collectively; management raised full-year revenue guidance to $85–87 billion, highlighted the U.S. Foundayo launch and Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program, positive phase III retatrutide results, and an active business development agenda including vaccine and psychiatry acquisitions.
keyTakeaways: Revenue grew 48% versus Q2 2025, with key products increasing by almost $6.8 billion.
MOUNJARO and ZEPBOUND combined for $14.9 billion of revenue, contributing $6.3 billion of growth year over year.

The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program launched July 1, giving 20 million eligible Americans coverage for obesity GLP-1s at $50 per month out of pocket, which management said expands coverage for Lilly obesity medicines by 35%.
Management said Foundayo U.S. prescribing reached an inflection in late July, with volume almost doubling versus a month earlier and prescribers rising from 8,000 to 36,000.
Three phase III retatrutide trials (TRIUMPH-1, -2, -3) read out positively, and management plans a U.S. submission in Q1 2027 under the BLA pathway, though BLA status is subject to active litigation.
Lilly announced acquisitions of Curevo, LimmaTech Biologics, The Vaccine Company and AtaiBeckley, expanding into infectious disease vaccines and psychiatry, and completed the Centessa acquisition.
Lilly holds approximately 55% share of the international incretin analog market, up almost 2 percentage points versus Q1 2026.

Regulatory milestones included FDA approval of Ebglyss every-eight-week maintenance dosing, EU approval of Jaypirca in CLL across all lines, and a positive CHMP opinion for insulin efsitora alfa (Onswik).
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 48% year over year in Q2 2026.
Gross margin was 86.3% of revenue, up about 1.3 percentage points, driven by product mix and lower production costs.
Marketing, selling and administrative expenses rose 25% and R&D expenses rose 14%.
Non-GAAP performance margin was 54.8%, up nine percentage points versus Q2 2025.
Non-GAAP EPS was $8.38 including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges, versus $6.31 (including $0.14 IPR&D) in Q2 2025.
U.S. revenue grew 33%, with U.S. price down 3% reported and down 9% excluding favorable rebate and discount estimate changes.
Europe revenue grew 55% in constant currency, including a $250 million Jardiance milestone payment.
Japan revenue grew 30%, China 93%, and rest of world 136%, all in constant currency.
Ebglyss worldwide sales more than doubled and Jaypirca worldwide sales grew 56% year over year.
INLURIYO holds more than 50% of U.S. new prescriptions in the oral SERD market after two full quarters.
U.S. incretin analog total prescriptions grew 31%, with obesity prescriptions up 78% and Type 2 diabetes prescriptions up 9%.
Lilly accounted for about six in 10 U.S. obesity incretin prescriptions and about seven in 10 injectable ones.
Self-pay accounted for about 45% of total ZEPBOUND prescriptions and about 55% of new prescriptions.
Lilly paid $1.5 billion in dividends and executed $1.6 billion of share repurchases in Q2.
An analyst cited Foundayo Q2 sales of $31 million in the UAE and $67 million in the U.S.
guidance: Management now expects full-year 2026 revenue of $85–87 billion, raising the low end by $3 billion and the high end by $2 billion.
Management now expects non-GAAP performance margin of 49%–50.5%, up 2 percentage points at both ends.
Management now expects non-GAAP EPS of $35.50–$36.50, a $2.78 increase at the midpoint before absorbing $3.03 of Q2 acquired IPR&D charges.
Management does not expect prior-period U.S. rebate and discount estimate adjustments to recur in the second half, and has factored in Q3 European and Q4 U.S. Type 2 diabetes seasonality.
Management expects regulatory action on Foundayo for Type 2 diabetes in the U.S. later this year and a global rollout in all major markets in 2027, with over 40 countries under review.
Management plans to submit retatrutide in the U.S. in Q1 2027.
Management expects the first Foundayo obstructive sleep apnea readout later this year, EMBER-4 adjuvant readout next year, and lebrikizumab every-12-week data in 2027.
Management expects European approval of insulin efsitora alfa in the coming months.
Management expects U.S. ZEPBOUND net price to decline as CVS access resumes in Q4 and medical exceptions fall, but expects volume growth to more than offset this.
analystFocus: Consumer and self-pay obesity market evolution in the U.S. versus internationally.
Pace of the U.S. Foundayo launch, sampling effects on IQVIA data, and competition from Novo Nordisk's oral in ex-U.S. markets including the UAE.
Retatrutide BLA pathway, litigation with FDA, competition from non-authentic product, and additional indications.
Early learnings from the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge rollout, including about 80% injectable preference and 60%–70% new patients.
Post-Verzenio breast cancer strategy and potential all-oral combinations.
Whether second-half guidance implies deceleration and whether it is conservative.
OUS MOUNJARO growth drivers and the impact of generic semaglutide in India, Brazil and Canada.
Sustainability of U.S. obesity net pricing and medical exceptions.
Strategic rationale for psychiatry and vaccine acquisitions.
Non-obesity pipeline highlights and Foundayo's ex-U.S. obesity and diabetes reimbursement potential.
risksMentioned: Actual results could differ materially from forward-looking statements due to factors in the 10-K and SEC filings.
Retatrutide BLA classification is subject to active litigation with a mixed initial court decision, and additional CMC data are still needed before filing.
U.S. price declined 9% excluding rebate estimate adjustments, and favorable prior-period adjustments are not expected to recur.
Management expects ZEPBOUND net price to decline as medical exceptions diminish with CVS access.
Generic semaglutide launches in markets such as India, Brazil and Canada, which management is monitoring.
Early Foundayo ex-U.S. data are noisy and include inventory build, and OUS reimbursement typically takes time.
Seasonality in Europe in Q3 and in U.S. Type 2 diabetes in Q4.
Tougher year-over-year comparison as the 2025 wave of new-country MOUNJARO launches will not repeat.
Availability of non-authentic retatrutide in the market.

parsed.overview: Deere reported fiscal Q3 2026 net sales and revenues up 5% to $12.608 billion and net income of $1.379 billion ($5.10 per diluted share), with equipment operations operating margin of 14.4%. Management raised full-year net income and cash flow guidance, narrowed segment margin ranges, and said it continues to believe 2026 is the bottom of the ag equipment cycle.
keyTakeaways: Equipment operations net sales rose 6% to $10.999 billion with a 14.4% operating margin.
Management said factories exceeded production expectations and results were above company and consensus expectations for revenue and profitability.
Production & Precision Ag sales fell 6% to $3.998 billion, while Small Ag & Turf rose 12% and Construction & Forestry rose 18%.
Management said it continues to believe 2026 represents the bottom of the ag equipment cycle and expects a measured, regionally varied recovery rather than a sharp rebound in 2027.
Early order programs for model year 2027 planters and sprayers were up mid-single digits versus last year's completed programs, though both were still open.

Technology adoption was highlighted: See & Spray expected on about one-third of North American sprayers on order, and over 40% of North American planters include advanced offerings for model year 2027.
C&F order books extend four to five months, above the typical two to three months, with customer backlogs extending well into fiscal 2027.
financialHighlights: Net income attributable to Deere was $1.379 billion, or $5.10 per diluted share.
Production & Precision Ag operating profit was $527 million (13.2% margin), with price realization of +2.5 points and currency of just over +1.5 points.
Small Ag & Turf operating profit was $622 million (18.4% margin), with price realization of a little over +1.5 points.
Construction & Forestry operating profit was $436 million (12.1% margin) on net sales of $3.618 billion, with price realization of +8 points.
Financial Services net income attributable to Deere was $219 million.
Management recognized $110 million of incremental IEEPA tariff refunds in Q3, bringing fiscal 2026 total refunds to $382 million.
Management expects direct tariff expense of about $1.1 billion for fiscal 2026 excluding refunds, down from a prior $1.2 billion.
guidance: Management now expects fiscal 2026 net income of $4.75 billion-$5 billion, with an effective tax rate of 24%-26%.
Management expects equipment operations operating cash flow of $5 billion-$5.5 billion.
Management expects Production & Precision Ag net sales down approximately 10% with operating margin of 11%-12%.
Management expects Small Ag & Turf net sales up approximately 15% with operating margin of 14.5%-15.5%.
Management expects Construction & Forestry net sales up approximately 20% with operating margin of 10.5%-11.5%.
Management expects Financial Services net income of $870 million for fiscal 2026.
Management expects Q4 net sales for PPA and C&F similar to Q3, with PPA and SAT margins lower on seasonally higher R&D and SA&G and no Q4 refund benefit.
Management expects a net tariff headwind in 2027, with a run rate of about $1 billion versus roughly $750 million net this year, and assumes no further refunds in the rest of fiscal 2026.
analystFocus: Production versus retail and pricing setup for 2027, including whether early order program pricing covers inflation.
Drivers of the change in tariff expectations and the net tariff impact for 2027 versus 2026.
Early order program cadence, regional variation, and technology take rates.
Construction & Forestry pricing, rental fleet growth, order backlog and the Deere-designed excavator launch.
Mix effects from technology adoption in 2027.
Europe demand outlook, including the potential effect of 2028 CAP policy change, and input cost effects on Brazilian and US farmers.
Q3-to-Q4 inventory and shipment cadence, and the right-to-repair FTC settlement's implications for lifecycle solutions.
risksMentioned: Management said farm profitability remains muted, with elevated input costs, commodity price volatility and uncertainty around crop demand and trade flows.
Management expects US and Canada large ag industry sales down 15%-20% and South America down 15%-20%, pressured by fertilizer costs and higher interest rates.
European arable farm profitability remains pressured by input costs and heat and drought uncertainty, with industry sales expected roughly flat.
Management said the inflationary environment is dynamic, including oil prices and supplier tariffs passed through.
Global forestry industry is expected down 10% on subdued residential construction and softer log and lumber prices.
Management cited too-early-to-tell uncertainty for 2027 in South America and Europe, and noted shipment disruptions such as the Black Sea.

parsed.overview: Chipotle reported Q2 fiscal 2026 revenue up 9.3% to $3.3 billion, with comparable sales up 2.2% (transactions +1%), restaurant-level margin of 25.2% (down 220 bps), and adjusted EPS of $0.33 (flat); management attributed momentum to its Recipe for Growth strategy, raised full-year comp guidance to low single digits, and flagged a roughly 200 bp softening in late July tied to industry-wide Cyclospora concerns.
keyTakeaways: Management credited transaction growth to the return of Chipotle Honey Chicken (cumulative attachment above 25%), Cilantro Lime Sauce, the mid-April rewards relaunch and Summer of Extras.

HEAP equipment is installed in more than 1,000 restaurants, with HEAP restaurants doing 2–3 more entrees in their peak 15 minutes; management expects about 2,000 by year-end and the full portfolio sometime in 2027.
Only about 20% of in-restaurant transactions scan for rewards versus nearly 90% of own digital transactions, and a frictionless pay-to-earn rewards pilot is planned for August.
New in-restaurant enrollment tools drove a nearly 20% step-up in daily rewards enrollments, and the program has 23 million active members.
Catering and Build-Your-Own Chipotle represent 2%–3% of sales, with management positioning for a national launch in 2027.
Matchday BOGO set a new single-day sales record and was the most successful BOGO in the company's history.
General manager turnover is at a multi-year low and crew turnover has returned to historical norms.
International expansion includes the first Monterrey, Mexico restaurant, with Seoul planned this year and Singapore in early 2027; Europe delivered high single-digit comps in each country.
New Chief Digital Officer Arlie Sisson and Chief Brand Officer Fernando Machado joined, with first elements of evolved brand messaging expected later this quarter.
Scott Boatwright stated Chipotle is not involved in the Cyclospora issue, as it does not use the implicated products and sources its lettuces in California.
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 9.3% to $3.3 billion.
Comparable restaurant sales rose 2.2%, including a 1% transaction comp.
Digital sales were $1.3 billion, or 38.3% of total sales, versus 35.5% a year ago.
Restaurant-level margin was 25.2%, down 220 basis points year-over-year.
Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.33, flat year-over-year.
The company opened 101 new restaurants, including 80 Chipotlanes and one international partner-operated restaurant.
Cost of sales was 29.7%, up about 80 bps, as beef and freight inflation and higher ingredient usage more than offset menu price and lower avocado and dairy costs.
Labor was 25%, up about 30 bps, on wage inflation, performance bonuses and guest-experience labor investment.
Other operating costs were 14.9%, up about 90 bps, with marketing at 3% of sales, up about 30 bps.
G&A was $190 million GAAP and $176 million non-GAAP.
Depreciation was $98 million, or 2.9% of sales.
The effective tax rate was 24.3% GAAP and 24.0% non-GAAP.
Pricing contributed about 1.6% in Q2.
Q2 buybacks totaled $631 million at an average price of $32.55, bringing the year-to-date total to over $1.3 billion at $34.35.
The board added $1.3 billion to the buyback authorization, leaving $1.7 billion remaining.
The quarter ended with $800 million in cash, restricted cash and investments, no debt and access to a $500 million revolver.
New restaurant productivity is in the 80% range and year-2 cash-on-cash returns are around 60%.
guidance: Management now expects full-year 2026 comp sales growth in the low single-digit range.
Management expects Q3 comps of around +1%, which assumes a continued roughly 200 bp Cyclospora-related impact on an underlying trend of about 3%.
Management expects pricing to rise to the mid-2% range in Q3, with the full year near the high end of the 1%–2% range.
Management expects Q3 cost of sales just under 30%, with low single-digit inflation of about 3%.
Management expects price and inflation to match from Q4 onward.
Management expects Q3 labor in the mid-25% range, with low single-digit wage inflation.
Management expects Q3 other operating costs in the mid-15% range, with marketing in the low 3% range for both Q3 and the full year.
Management expects Q3 non-GAAP G&A of about $180 million, comprising $152 million underlying, $25 million stock compensation and $3 million in bonus and payroll taxes.
Management expects 2026 depreciation of around 3% of sales and an underlying tax rate of 24%–26%.
Management expects about 350 restaurant openings in 2026, about 80% with a Chipotlane, and sees potential for at least 7,000 North American restaurants.
Management plans two additional limited-time protein options in the second half, plus sides and beverage innovation.
Management is planning an investor event in the new year.
analystFocus: Whether repeat LTOs keep delivering lift, and how value perception is trending; management said Honey Chicken performed better the second time and affordability scores were the best in a couple of years.
Confidence in momentum building into 2027 given the spending required to generate 1%–2% comps.
Q3 comp cadence and the Cyclospora impact.
Remodel testing at $100,000–$300,000 per restaurant and the partner-operated international model; management said it will own and operate Western Europe and use partners elsewhere.
Digital sales drivers, which an analyst put at roughly 18% growth.
Whether HEAP labor savings of about 2–4 hours are reinvested; management said yes.
Why 350 openings a year is the right pace rather than 400.
Brand messaging direction under the new CMO.
Max 15 throughput, which management put at the low 20s in-store, mid-teens digital and low-to-mid 30s combined.
Loyalty adoption in-restaurant and whether non-members skew to lower-income guests; management said they do not.
Upcoming menu items across center-of-plate, sides, beverages and desserts.
Trends by age and income cohort; younger and lower-income guests improved the most, and the company has taken share in each month of 2026.
The margin outlook and the gap between price and inflation.
World Cup impact, which management said was under 5 bps for the quarter.
Learnings from the rolling pricing approach.
LTO contribution to traffic; management cited hundreds of basis points of transaction lift.
risksMentioned: Trends softened by about 200 bps in the second half of July amid industry Cyclospora concerns and heightened consumer caution, with uncertain duration.
Q3 is the toughest comparison of the year as the company laps increased prior-year promotional activity.
Inflation in beef, freight, insurance, maintenance and utilities, plus higher wages, pressured margins.
Middle East development remains dependent on geopolitical conditions.
Management noted possible diminishing returns from repeated LTOs and from opening more than about 350 restaurants a year.
Forward-looking statements are subject to the risk factors in the company's 10-K and 10-Q filings.

parsed.overview: Eli Lilly reported Q2 2026 revenue growth of 48% year over year, driven primarily by Mounjaro and Zepbound, with non-GAAP EPS of $8.38 including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges. Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $85–87 billion, highlighted continued momentum in the U.S. Foundayo launch and first international approvals, reported positive phase III retatrutide results, and announced multiple acquisitions expanding into vaccines and psychiatry.
keyTakeaways: Revenue grew 48% versus Q2 2025, with key products up almost $6.8 billion and oncology, immunology and neuroscience medicines collectively growing 121%.
Mounjaro and Zepbound combined for $14.9 billion of revenue, contributing $6.3 billion of year-over-year growth.
Management raised full-year revenue guidance to $85–87 billion and non-GAAP EPS guidance to $35.50–$36.50.
The U.S. Foundayo launch gained commercial access across all three major PBMs in June, broad DTC marketing began, and management said prescriber count rose from 8,000 to 36,000.
Foundayo launched for obesity in the UAE, received approvals in Saudi Arabia (obesity) and Mexico (obesity and Type 2 diabetes), and is under review in over 40 additional countries.
Three phase III retatrutide trials (TRIUMPH-1, -2, -3) read out positively, and management plans a U.S. submission in Q1 2027 under the BLA pathway.
The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program launched July 1, giving 20 million eligible Americans coverage at $50 per month out-of-pocket, which management said expands U.S. obesity coverage by 35%.
Lilly announced acquisitions of Curevo, LimmaTech Biologics, The Vaccine Company (vaccines) and AtaiBeckley (treatment-resistant depression), and completed the Centessa acquisition.

Pirtobrutinib (Jaypirca) in BRUIN CLL-322 reduced risk of progression or death by 45% overall and 68% in patients progressing after a prior covalent BTK inhibitor; selpercatinib in LIBRETTO-432 reduced risk of recurrence or death by 83%.
Lilly distributed $1.5 billion in dividends and executed $1.6 billion in share repurchases during the quarter.
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 48% year over year, driven by Zepbound and Mounjaro.
Gross margin was 86.3% of revenue, up approximately 1.3 percentage points, on favorable product mix and improved cost of production.
Marketing, selling and administrative expenses rose 25%; R&D expenses rose 14% with more than 40 active phase III programs.
Non-GAAP performance margin was 54.8%, up nine percentage points from Q2 2025.
Non-GAAP EPS was $8.38 including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges, versus $6.31 a year ago including $0.14 of such charges.
U.S. revenue grew 33%, primarily on volume; U.S. price declined 3%, or 9% excluding a favorable change in rebate and discount estimates.
Europe revenue grew 55% in constant currency, including a $250 million Jardiance milestone payment; Japan grew 30%, China 93%, and rest of world 136% in constant currency.
Mounjaro and Zepbound combined for $14.9 billion of revenue; Ebglyss worldwide sales more than doubled; Jaypirca worldwide sales rose 56%.
Foundayo generated $67 million in the U.S. and $31 million in the UAE in the quarter, per an analyst's figures that management did not dispute.
U.S. incretin analog total prescriptions grew 31%, obesity market prescriptions grew 78%, and self-pay accounted for about 45% of total and 55% of new Zepbound prescriptions.
International incretin analog market grew 74% by IQVIA gross sales, with Lilly share reaching approximately 55%, up almost 2 percentage points from Q1 2026.
guidance: Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $85 billion–$87 billion, increasing the low end by $3 billion and the high end by $2 billion.
Management now expects non-GAAP performance margin of 49%–50.5%, up 2 percentage points at both ends of the range.
Management now expects non-GAAP EPS of $35.50–$36.50, an increase of $2.78 at the midpoint before the $3.03 Q2 acquired IPR&D charge.
Management expects U.S. regulatory action on Foundayo for Type 2 diabetes later this year and a global Foundayo rollout in all major markets in 2027.
Management plans to submit retatrutide in the U.S. in Q1 2027 under the BLA pathway.
Management expects the first Foundayo obstructive sleep apnea readout later this year, with five additional phase III programs ongoing.
Management expects European approval of insulin efsitora alfa (Onswik) in the coming months and EMBER-4 adjuvant data for Inluriyo next year.

Management said favorable rebate/discount adjustments are not expected to recur in the second half, and Zepbound net price is expected to decline as CVS access takes effect in Q4, with volume more than offsetting.
analystFocus: Consumer and self-pay strategy for obesity in the U.S. versus international markets.
Pace of the U.S. Foundayo launch and competitive dynamics ex-U.S. versus Novo Nordisk's oral, including UAE share.
Retatrutide's BLA versus NDA regulatory pathway and the ongoing litigation with FDA.
Early learnings from the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge rollout, including the oral-versus-injectable mix (management cited about 80% injectable, 60–70% new patients).
Whether second-half guidance implies a deceleration, which management attributed to non-recurring rebate adjustments, prior-year launch bolus, and seasonality.
Ex-U.S. Mounjaro performance and impact of generic semaglutide in India, Brazil and Canada.
Foundayo sampling effects on IQVIA data and prescriber base expansion.
Sustainability of Zepbound net pricing and medical-exception dynamics with CVS returning to formulary.
Rationale for M&A expansion into psychiatry and vaccines.
Pipeline assets outside obesity and Foundayo's ex-U.S. obesity and diabetes reimbursement potential.
risksMentioned: Standard forward-looking statement caveats referencing factors in the Form 10-K and SEC filings.
Active litigation over FDA's determination of retatrutide's BLA pathway, with additional CMC data still needed before submission.
U.S. price declines on Zepbound and Mounjaro, and management's expectation that net price will fall further as CVS access resumes.
Favorable rebate and discount estimate adjustments that are not expected to recur in the second half of 2026.
Seasonality in Europe in Q3 and in U.S. Type 2 diabetes in Q4, factored into guidance.
Generic semaglutide launches in India, Brazil and Canada, which management said has not yet slowed Mounjaro prescriptions.
Competitive oral GLP-1 entry from Novo Nordisk in the UAE and other ex-U.S. markets.
Noise and inventory build in early ex-U.S. Foundayo launch data.
Unauthorized retatrutide product apparently available in the market ahead of approval, which management expects authentic product to displace.
Ex-U.S. reimbursement for Foundayo expected to take time, with early launches focused on self-pay chronic weight management.

parsed.overview: Kinsale reported Q2 2026 diluted operating EPS of $5.54 (up 15.9% from $4.78), a 75.5% combined ratio and 24.4% annualized operating ROE, while gross written premium fell 5% amid a competitive E&S market, especially in its Commercial Property Division (larger layered accounts); management emphasised profitability over growth, technology/AI efficiency, and expanded its buyback authorization by $250 million to $337 million.
keyTakeaways: Management said E&S conditions in Q2 were competitive and largely consistent with Q1, with competition most intense in the Commercial Property Division, which it described as a buyer's market.
Excluding the Commercial Property Division, gross written premium grew 3.7% in the quarter and 4.8% in the first half.
New business submissions rose 6% overall and 8% excluding the Commercial Property Division, with over half of divisions seeing double-digit submission growth.

Growth areas cited included excess casualty, commercial auto, Entertainment, Environmental, Agribusiness Casualty and Energy, while Commercial Property, Construction and certain Professional Lines were described as soft.
Management reiterated it will not sacrifice profitability for top-line growth and views losing accounts on price or terms as the model working as intended.
The buyback authorization was expanded by $250 million to $337 million, which management called its principal capital allocation strategy while growth is more limited.
Management highlighted AI adoption, including enterprise licenses for two frontier models for every associate and AI built into proprietary underwriting worksheets.
Nine new products or enhancements have launched this year, with five more imminent and 10 in the pipeline; 24 new wholesale brokers and 176 new retail brokers to Aspera were appointed.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS was $5.54 versus $4.78 in Q2 2025, up 15.9%.
Annualized operating ROE was 24.4%.
Gross written premium fell 5%, net written premium fell 1.4%, and net earned premium rose 8.9%.
Net income rose 31.1% and net operating earnings rose 13.3% year over year.
Combined ratio was 75.5%, including 4.5 points of net favorable prior-year reserve development (vs 3.9 points) and 1.3 points of cat losses (vs under 1 point).
Expense ratio was 21.7% versus 20.7%, driven by a higher net commission ratio from higher reinsurance retentions; the other underwriting expense ratio improved to 10.3% from 10.6%.
Net investment income rose 19.9%, and float grew to $3.4 billion at June 30 from $3.1 billion at year-end 2025.
Annualized gross investment return was 4.5% for the first half versus 4.3%, with new money yields around 5.25% and fixed maturity duration of about 4.25 years.
Average account premium is approximately $12,000, with the most meaningful growth from accounts of $25,000 and below.
guidance: Management said year-over-year growth comparisons become modestly easier in the next two quarters because 60% of Commercial Property Division premium was written in the first half of last year.

The CFO indicated the Q2 expense ratio should be a good measure going forward, with a possible slight uptick in commissions after the June 1 reinsurance renewal partly offset by potential AI-driven operating efficiencies.
Management said the current accident year loss ratio could drift up over time given mix shift, though losses are coming in below expectations.
Management said it will continue to lean into buybacks, with roughly $80 million remaining on the prior authorization plus the new $250 million, and would prioritise growth if it accelerates.
Management expects new products to contribute growth at a slow, crawl-walk-run pace.
analystFocus: Drivers of the improved current accident year loss ratio, which management attributed to normal variability and mix, with short-tail lines performing especially well.
Reinsurance ceding commission outlook after the June 1 renewal.
ROE compression in E&S casualty, with management noting it manages to a 20% or greater ROE.
Broker commission pressure and tension in the soft market.
Whether commercial property pricing has troughed, which management said it could not predict, citing continued pressure from London MGAs.
Causes of the ex-property growth trend and whether business is returning to the admitted market, which management said is occurring but not pervasive.
Social inflation and casualty loss trends, which management put at mid-single digits.
Pacing of share buybacks and contribution from new products.
risksMentioned: Intense competition and material rate declines with expanding coverage in large layered commercial property.
Competitors underpricing risk and stretching terms in a soft market.
London MGA competition spreading into long-tail casualty and Construction lines, depressing pricing.
The MS Amlin pricing index showed a 5.9% decrease versus 3.3% in Q1 2026, with Kinsale's combined pricing trend in line.
Possible upward drift in the accident year loss ratio from mix shift away from property.
Higher net commission ratio from increased reinsurance retentions.
Some flow of business back to the admitted market and broker commission tension.
Intermittent and unpredictable catastrophe losses.

parsed.overview: Chipotle reported fiscal Q2 2026 revenue growth of 9.3% to $3.3 billion with comparable restaurant sales up 2.2% and transactions up 1%, while restaurant level margin declined 220 basis points to 25.2% and adjusted diluted EPS was flat at $0.33. Management attributed the transaction growth to its Recipe for Growth strategy, including the return of Chipotle Honey Chicken, Cilantro Lime Sauce, the relaunched rewards program, and the rollout of the High-Efficiency Equipment Package (HEAP), and raised full-year comp guidance to low single digits despite a roughly 200 basis point softening in late July that management linked to the industry-wide Cyclospora issue.
keyTakeaways: Management said transaction comp was positive at 1% and improved through the quarter, with momentum continuing into the first half of July before softening by about 200 basis points in the second half of July.

HEAP is installed in more than 1,000 restaurants, and management said HEAP restaurants outperform the enterprise by 2 to 3 entrees in their peak 15-minute period, translating into hundreds of basis points of comp improvement.
Chipotle Honey Chicken outperformed last year's launch with a cumulative attachment rate above 25%, and Cilantro Lime Sauce attachment remains above Red Chimichurri and Adobo Ranch.

The rewards relaunch in mid-April drove a nearly 20% step-up in daily enrollments, and management noted only about 20% of in-restaurant transactions scan for rewards versus nearly 90% of own digital transactions.
Management said the Matchday BOGO set a new single-day sales record and was the most successful BOGO in company history.
Management said Chipotle gained wallet share in each month of 2026 across all income cohorts and age groups, with the younger and lower-income cohorts improving the most.
Catering and Build-Your-Own Chipotle represent 2%-3% of sales today, and management is positioning for a national catering launch in 2027.
Management said general manager turnover is at a multi-year low and crew turnover has returned to historical norms.

Management opened the first restaurant in Monterrey, Mexico with partner Alsea, plans first openings in Seoul this year and Singapore in early 2027 with SPC Group, and said Middle East sales are returning to pre-conflict levels.
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 9.3% to $3.3 billion with comparable restaurant sales up 2.2% and transaction comp of 1%.
Digital sales were $1.3 billion, or 38.3% of total sales, versus 35.5% in the prior year.
Restaurant level margin was 25.2%, down 220 basis points year-over-year.
Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.33, flat to last year.
Cost of sales was 29.7%, up about 80 basis points, as beef and freight inflation and higher ingredient usage more than offset menu price and lower avocado and dairy costs.
Labor costs were 25%, up about 30 basis points, driven by wage inflation, performance bonuses, and hospitality investments.
Other operating costs were 14.9%, up about 90 basis points, with marketing at 3% of sales, up about 30 basis points.
G&A was $190 million on a GAAP basis, or $176 million non-GAAP, including $148 million of underlying G&A and $25 million of non-cash stock compensation.
Depreciation was $98 million, or 2.9% of sales; the effective tax rate was 24.3% GAAP and 24.0% non-GAAP.
Menu pricing impact was around 1.6% in Q2.
The company opened 101 new restaurants, including 80 Chipotlanes and one international partner-operated restaurant.

Cash, restricted cash, and investments ended at $800 million, down $1.3 billion year-over-year, with $631 million of stock repurchased in Q2 at an average price of $32.55 and over $1.3 billion year-to-date at $34.35.
The board authorized an additional $1.3 billion in repurchases, leaving $1.7 billion remaining, with a $500 million revolver and no debt.
guidance: Management now expects full-year 2026 comparable sales growth in the low single-digit range.
Management expects Q3 comps of around plus 1%, assuming the roughly 200 basis point Cyclospora-related headwind continues through the quarter against the toughest lap of the year.
Management expects pricing to rise to the mid 2% range in Q3 and full-year pricing to land near the high end of the 1%-2% range.

Management anticipates Q3 cost of sales just under 30% with low single-digit inflation, labor in the mid 25% range with low single-digit wage inflation, other operating costs in the mid 15% range, and marketing in the low 3% range for Q3 and the full year.
Management expects Q3 non-GAAP G&A of around $180 million, including $152 million underlying, $25 million stock compensation, and $3 million higher bonus accruals and payroll taxes.
Management expects depreciation around 3% of sales for 2026 and an underlying effective tax rate of 24%-26%.
Management expects Q3 inflation near 3% versus mid-2% pricing, with pricing and inflation expected to match from Q4 onward.

Management still expects approximately 350 restaurant openings in 2026 with about 80% including a Chipotlane, and HEAP in approximately 2,000 restaurants by year-end with the full portfolio completed sometime in 2027.

Management plans two additional limited-time protein options in the second half, a frictionless in-restaurant rewards pilot in August, additional Monterrey openings this year, and Mexico City expansion in 2027.
analystFocus: Whether repeat LTOs like Chipotle Honey Chicken deliver lifts as strong as prior runs and how value perception is trending.
Why management is confident momentum will build into 2027 given the spending behind 1%-2% comps and recent softening.
The composition of the Q3 comp guide, including the roughly 200 basis point Cyclospora impact and implied underlying trend of about 3%.
Remodel/refresh program economics, with management citing $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant test investments but no results yet, and use of partners versus company ownership internationally.
Drivers of digital sales growth and the link to loyalty and in-store payment friction.
HEAP labor reinvestment and system-wide Max 15 throughput, which management put at low 20s in-store and low to mid-30s including digital.
Why 350 openings per year is viewed as the right pace versus a prior 400 ceiling.
Direction of brand messaging under the new Chief Brand Officer and emphasis on value and ingredient quality.
Trends by age and income cohort, the margin outlook and pricing-versus-inflation gap, World Cup impact, and LTO contribution to frequency and new guest acquisition.
risksMentioned: Management cited softer trends in late July amid heightened consumer caution and the industry-wide Cyclospora issue, estimated at about a 200 basis point comp impact with uncertain duration.
Q3 comparisons are more difficult as the company laps increased prior-year promotional activity.
Inflation in beef, freight, insurance, maintenance, and utilities, with sequentially higher avocado pricing expected in Q3.
Near-term development in the Middle East remains dependent on geopolitical conditions.
Management noted possible diminishing returns from repeatedly bringing back the same LTOs and a risk of fracturing the base if openings accelerate too aggressively beyond 350 per year.
Standard forward-looking statement caution that actual results could differ materially from projections.

parsed.overview: Deere reported a strong fiscal Q3 2026, with net sales and revenues up 5% to $12.608 billion, equipment operations operating margin of 14.4%, and net income of $1.379 billion ($5.10 per diluted share); management raised full-year net income guidance to $4.75–$5.0 billion, citing strength in Construction & Forestry and Small Ag & Turf offsetting softer large ag demand in South America and Europe, and reiterated its view that 2026 represents the bottom of the ag equipment cycle.
keyTakeaways: Diversification supported results: Small Ag & Turf sales rose 12% and C&F sales rose 18%, while Production & Precision Ag sales fell 6%.
Management raised FY2026 net income guidance to $4.75–$5.0 billion and equipment operations cash flow to $5.0–$5.5 billion.
North American model year 2027 early order programs for planters and sprayers are running up mid-single digits versus last year's completed programs, which management views as an encouraging signal.
Management believes 2026 is the bottom of the ag equipment cycle but expects a measured recovery rather than a sharp rebound in 2027.

C&F order books are four to five months out, customer backlogs extend into fiscal 2027, and Deere is modestly underproducing retail demand in both C&F and PPA (roughly a couple of percentage points each).
Channel inventory has improved, with model-year 2023 and 2024 high-horsepower tractor used inventory down nearly 40% from a year ago.

Precision tech adoption is rising: See & Spray is on about one-third of North American sprayers on order (nearly double factory adoption), and over 40% of MY2027 North American planters include advanced offerings.
Direct tariff expense for FY2026 is now expected at about $1.1 billion (down from $1.2 billion), mainly due to Section 232 rate changes, with $382 million of refunds recognized year-to-date.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues rose 5% to $12.608 billion; equipment operations net sales rose 6% to $10.999 billion.
Net income attributable to Deere was $1.379 billion, or $5.10 per diluted share.
Equipment operations operating margin was 14.4%.
Production & Precision Ag net sales fell 6% to $3.998 billion, with operating profit of $527 million and a 13.2% margin; price realization was +2.5 points and currency about +1.5 points.
Small Ag & Turf net sales rose 12% to $3.383 billion, with operating profit of $622 million and an 18.4% margin; price was a little over +1.5 points and currency about -0.5 points.

Construction & Forestry net sales rose 18% to $3.618 billion, with operating profit of $436 million and a 12.1% margin; price realization was +8 points, partly from lapping roughly -5% price in Q3 2025.
Financial Services net income attributable to Deere was $219 million.
Q3 included $110 million of tariff refunds, bringing FY2026 refunds recognized to $382 million.
C&F technology momentum: factory-installed SmartGrade adoption is up more than 50% year-to-date, and job site safety solution sales are up nearly 40% year-over-year.
Operations Center has more than 520 million engaged acres, nearly 1.2 million connected machines, more than 190 million highly engaged acres, and more than 450,000 monthly active digital users.
guidance: Management raised FY2026 net income guidance to $4.75–$5.0 billion, with an effective tax rate of 24%–26%.
Management expects FY2026 equipment operations operating cash flow of $5.0–$5.5 billion.
For PPA, management expects net sales down about 10%, including +1 point of price and about +2.5 points of currency, with operating margin of 11%–12%.
For Small Ag & Turf, management expects net sales up about 15%, including +1.5 points of price and about +0.5 point of currency, with operating margin raised to 14.5%–15.5%.
For C&F, management expects net sales up about 20%, including +3 points of price and about +1.5 points of currency, with operating margin of 10.5%–11.5%.
Management raised its Financial Services FY2026 net income outlook to $870 million.
Industry outlook: U.S./Canada large ag down 15%–20%; U.S./Canada small ag and turf flat to up 5%; Europe about flat; South America down 15%–20%; Asia about flat.
C&F industry outlook: U.S./Canada construction equipment up 5%–10%; compact construction up 5%; global forestry down 10%; global road building up about 10%.
Management expects Q4 net sales for PPA and C&F to be similar to Q3, with lower margins in PPA and Small Ag & Turf due to no refunds and seasonally higher R&D and SA&G.
The outlook assumes no further tariff refunds in FY2026.
Management expects a net tariff run rate of about $1 billion in FY2027, compared with roughly $750 million net in FY2026, implying a step up in tariff expense.
analystFocus: 2027 production-versus-retail setup and early order program pricing; management said pricing aims to cover inflation.
Drivers of the tariff estimate change from $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion, and whether net tariffs are a headwind or tailwind into 2027.
Progress of the Deere-designed excavator launch, with three models in market and further rollout over the next three to four years.
Q3-to-Q4 inventory and shipment cadence, including some demand pulled into Q3 to manage Q4 risk.
Potential 2027 mix impact from higher technology take rates; management said it is too early to tell.
Regional variation and order cadence in the early order programs, with the U.S. trending slightly better than Canada.
8R tractor orders (as expected), the Europe outlook, and Brazil's three-month order book.
C&F order trends and dealer rental fleet expansion, with 30%–35% of earthmoving transactions starting as rentals.
C&F pricing cadence after the +8 points in Q3.
Implications of the FTC settlement on right to repair for the aftermarket and lifecycle solutions business.
Whether the EU CAP policy change in 2028 could pull forward or delay European demand.
How fertilizer and other input costs are shaping decisions by U.S. and Brazilian farmers.
risksMentioned: Muted farm profitability, elevated input costs (especially fertilizer), and commodity price volatility weighing on ag capital spending.
Higher interest rates and production costs pressuring South American farm economics.
Pressure on European arable farm profitability, plus heat and drought uncertainty.
Subdued residential construction and softer log and lumber prices weighing on forestry demand.
Tariff exposure, including a net tariff step up expected in 2027 and supplier tariff pass-through.
A dynamic inflationary environment, including oil price moves.
Shipment disruptions such as those in the Black Sea, and uncertainty around trade flows.
Higher production costs and seasonally higher R&D and SA&G pressuring margins.
EU CAP policy uncertainty in 2028.

parsed.overview: Kinsale Capital Group reported Q2 2026 diluted operating EPS of $5.54, up 15.9% year over year, with a 75.5% combined ratio and a 24.4% annualized operating ROE, despite gross written premium declining 5% as management prioritised profitability over growth in a competitive E&S market, particularly in the Commercial Property Division. Excluding Commercial Property, gross written premium grew 3.7% in the quarter, and management expanded the share buyback authorization by $250 million to a total of $337 million.
keyTakeaways: Management said E&S market conditions remained competitive and largely consistent with Q1, with competition most intense in the Commercial Property Division where larger layered accounts are seeing material rate declines and expanding coverage.

Excluding the Commercial Property Division, gross written premium grew 3.7% in the quarter and 4.8% in the first half, with new business submissions up 8% and over half of divisions seeing double-digit submission growth.

Management stated it prioritises profitability over growth and will not sacrifice margins for top-line growth, viewing lost accounts due to competitor pricing or terms as the model working as intended.
Lines with favourable underwriting conditions and meaningful growth included excess casualty, commercial auto, Entertainment, Environmental, Agribusiness Casualty and Energy.
Kinsale's combined pricing trend was in line with the MS Amlin pricing index, which showed a 5.9% decrease versus a 3.3% decrease in Q1 2026.
The company rolled out nine new product offerings or enhancements year to date, appointed 24 new wholesale brokers and 176 new retail brokers to Aspera, its in-house broker for personal lines.
Management emphasised technology and AI as core competencies, with every associate licensed for two frontier AI models and AI built into proprietary underwriting worksheets.
The buyback authorization was expanded by $250 million to $337 million, which management described as its principal capital allocation strategy while growth is more limited.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS was $5.54 versus $4.78 in Q2 2025, an increase of 15.9%.
Net income and net operating earnings increased 31.1% and 13.3% respectively year over year.
Annualized operating return on equity was 24.4%.
Gross written premium declined 5%, net written premium declined 1.4%, and net earned premium increased 8.9%.
Combined ratio was 75.5%, including 4.5 points of net favorable prior year reserve development (vs 3.9 points last year) and 1.3 points of cat losses (vs less than a point last year).

Expense ratio was 21.7% versus 20.7% a year ago, with the other underwriting expense portion at 10.3% versus 10.6%; the increase was attributed to a higher net commission ratio from higher reinsurance retentions.
Net investment income increased 19.9% year over year.
Float grew to $3.4 billion at June 30 from $3.1 billion at end of 2025.
Annualized gross investment return was 4.5% for the first half of 2026 versus 4.3% last year, with new money yields around 5.25% and a fixed maturity duration of 4.25 years.
Average account premium is approximately $12,000, with the most meaningful growth in accounts of $25,000 and below.
Management noted roughly $80 million remained on the prior $250 million authorization before the new $250 million authorization.
guidance: Management expects the year-over-year growth comparison to become modestly easier in the next two quarters because 60% of Commercial Property Division premium was written in the first half of last year.
Management indicated the Q2 expense ratio should be a good measure going forward, with a possible slight uptick in the commission ratio partly offset by potential AI-driven operating efficiencies.
Management said the current accident year loss ratio could drift up over time given mix shift, but losses are coming in below expectations and it feels good about current loss picks.
Management expects to continue leaning into buybacks in the interim phase of limited growth, but would prioritise growth over buybacks if growth accelerates.
Management expects new products to drive growth at a crawl-walk-run pace, ramping up as the market turns.
Management manages all product lines to a 20% or greater ROE target and said most lines are likely running ahead of that.
analystFocus: Drivers of the improved current accident year loss ratio and whether it was property-driven or across the board.
Outlook for the ceding commission rate following June 1 reinsurance renewals.
ROE compression in E&S casualty as the segment softens.
Broker commission pressure in a soft market and whether business is flowing to the admitted market.
Whether Q2 represents a trough in commercial property pricing and when equilibrium might be reached.
Sources of the increase in inbound accounts (broker re-engagement versus pricing).
Views on social inflation and casualty loss cost trends.
Sustainability of the underlying accident year loss ratio given the mix shift away from property.
Pacing of share buybacks going forward.
Contribution of new product rollouts to growth.
risksMentioned: Intense competition and material rate declines with expanding coverage in the Commercial Property Division, leading to shrinking volume there.
Competitors underpricing risk in the current soft market, with pressure from London MGAs and traditional markets putting up larger limits.

Competition in long-tail lines from London beginning to creep into other liability occurrence lines and depressing Construction pricing, with more competition emerging in general casualty and Inland Marine.
Tension over broker commission splits in a soft market, with some business flowing to the admitted market though not pervasively.
Casualty loss cost trends of mid-single digits, varying by line, though management said it sees limited social inflation exposure due to smaller accounts and lower limits.
Possible upward drift in the current accident year loss ratio over time due to mix shift.
Catastrophe losses described as intermittent and unpredictable, with management unable to say when property pricing equilibrium will arrive.

parsed.overview: Deere reported fiscal Q3 2026 net sales and revenues of $12.608 billion (up 5%) and net income of $1.379 billion ($5.10 per diluted share), with equipment operations operating margin of 14.4%, as strength in Construction & Forestry and Small Ag & Turf offset lower Production & Precision Ag volumes amid softer demand in South America and Europe; management raised full-year net income guidance to $4.75-$5 billion, lifted equipment operations cash flow guidance to $5-$5.5 billion, and reiterated its view that 2026 represents the bottom of the ag equipment cycle with a measured recovery expected rather than a sharp rebound.
keyTakeaways: Management raised fiscal 2026 net income guidance to $4.75-$5 billion and equipment operations cash flow guidance to $5-$5.5 billion, citing strong Q3 execution and a strong fourth-quarter order book across all segments.

Management continues to believe 2026 represents the bottom of the ag equipment cycle, with model year 2027 early order program intake for planters and sprayers running up mid-single digits versus the completion of last year's program.

Production & Precision Ag full-year sales guidance moved to down approximately 10% (bottom of prior range) on further industry softening in South America and Europe, with the South America industry outlook now down 15%-20% and Europe now approximately flat.

Construction & Forestry demand is strong, with order books largely full, four to five months of orders on hand, customer backlogs extending well into fiscal 2027, and the U.S./Canada construction equipment industry outlook raised to up 5%-10%.

Deere recognized $110 million of incremental IEPA tariff refunds in Q3 (total $382 million for fiscal 2026) and now expects direct tariff expense of approximately $1.1 billion for the year, down from $1.2 billion, due to Section 232 changes.

Precision technology adoption is accelerating, with See & Spray factory adoption expected to nearly double (on about one-third of North American sprayers on order) and more than 40% of North American model year 2027 planters taking advanced offerings.

Channel inventory has improved, with model year 2023 and 2024 used high-horsepower tractors down nearly 40% year-over-year and the new-to-used value spread largely normalized, while Deere is modestly underproducing retail demand in PPA and C&F.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues rose 5% to $12.608 billion; equipment operations net sales rose 6% to $10.999 billion; net income attributable to Deere was $1.379 billion or $5.10 per diluted share.
Equipment operations operating margin was 14.4%.
Production & Precision Ag net sales fell 6% to $3.998 billion with operating profit of $527 million and a 13.2% margin; price realization was +2.5 points and currency +1.5 points.
Small Ag & Turf net sales rose 12% to $3.383 billion with operating profit of $622 million and an 18.4% margin; price realization was +1.5 points and currency roughly -0.5 points.

Construction & Forestry net sales rose 18% to $3.618 billion with operating profit of $436 million and a 12.1% margin; price realization was +8 points, reflecting the lap of prior-year retail incentive programs.
Financial Services net income was $219 million, higher year-over-year on favorable financing spreads partially offset by a lower average portfolio.
Q3 included $110 million of incremental IEPA tariff refunds, bringing fiscal 2026 refunds recognized to $382 million.
Factory-installed SmartGrade adoption is up more than 50% year-to-date and job site safety solution sales are up nearly 40% year-over-year.

The Operations Center has more than 520 million engaged acres across nearly 1.2 million connected machines, with highly engaged acres above 190 million (double-digit growth) and more than 450,000 unique active monthly digital users.
guidance: Management raised fiscal 2026 net income guidance to $4.75-$5 billion, with an effective tax rate of 24%-26%.
Management raised equipment operations cash flow guidance to $5-$5.5 billion.
Management raised the fiscal 2026 Financial Services net income outlook to $870 million.
Production & Precision Ag net sales are now expected to be down approximately 10% with operating margin narrowed to 11%-12%, including 1 point of price and roughly 2.5 points of favorable currency.
Small Ag & Turf net sales are expected to be up approximately 15% with operating margin raised to 14.5%-15.5%, including 1.5 points of price and roughly 0.5 point of favorable currency.

Construction & Forestry net sales are expected to be up approximately 20% with operating margin tightened to 10.5%-11.5%, including 3 points of price and approximately 1.5 points of favorable currency.

Industry outlooks: U.S./Canada large ag down 15%-20%; U.S./Canada small ag and turf flat to up 5%; Europe approximately flat; South America down 15%-20%; Asia approximately flat; U.S./Canada construction equipment up 5%-10%; compact construction up 5%; global forestry down 10%; global road building up approximately 10%.

Management expects direct tariff expense of approximately $1.1 billion for fiscal 2026 excluding IEPA refunds, with no further refund activity assumed for the balance of the year, and a net tariff run rate closer to $1 billion in fiscal 2027, making tariffs a headwind next year.
Management expects Q4 net sales for PPA and C&F to be similar to Q3, but margins to come in somewhat lower for PPA and SAT due to no refund benefit and seasonally higher R&D and SA&G.
Management expects a measured rather than sharp ag recovery in 2027, dependent on farm economics, commodity prices, input cost stability, and renewable fuel demand.
analystFocus: Production versus retail by region and pricing for 2027, with management indicating a couple of points of underproduction in PPA and C&F this year and EOP pricing aimed at covering inflation.
Tariff dynamics, including the reduction from $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion in direct tariff expense and whether net tariffs will be a headwind or tailwind in 2027.
Progress of the Deere-designed excavator launch, with three models in market and positive early customer feedback.
Q3 inventory build and the Q3-to-Q4 bridge, with management saying it pulled ahead some demand to manage Q4 risk and that shipment plans are set.
Early order program cadence, regional variability (U.S. trending slightly better than Canada) and whether the mid-single-digit increase could strengthen as programs close.
Mix impact in 2027 from technology adoption and segment growth, which management said is too early to call.
C&F order trends and the contribution of dealer-owned rental fleets, with management noting 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as a rental.
C&F pricing moving from +8% in Q3 to a full-year guide of 3 points, explained by easy comps against roughly 5% negative price in Q3 2025.
The FTC settlement on right to repair and implications for the lifecycle solutions business.
Potential pull-forward or delay of European demand ahead of the 2028 policy change, and farmer responses to input cost uncertainty in Brazil and the U.S.
risksMentioned: Muted farm profitability and uncertainty around input costs, commodity price volatility, and crop demand weighing on large ag equipment demand in the U.S. and Canada.
Elevated production costs (particularly fertilizer) and higher interest rates pressuring farm economics and equipment affordability in South America.
Pressured arable farm profitability in Europe amid elevated input costs and heat and drought uncertainty.
Tariff expense of approximately $1.1 billion in fiscal 2026, with net tariffs expected to be a headwind in fiscal 2027 and no further refunds assumed.
Higher production costs cited as a partial offset in both ag segments, and higher SA&G and R&D costs in C&F.
A dynamic inflationary environment, including oil prices and suppliers passing through tariff costs.
Shipment disruptions, including references to the Black Sea, and trade flow uncertainty for crop production.
Subdued residential construction activity and softer log and lumber prices weighing on forestry equipment demand.
Policy uncertainty in Europe ahead of the 2028 cap budget change that could pull forward or delay purchases.
